title: Models of Computation: Languages, Machines & Logic
subtitle: From finite memory to the limits of algorithms, with logic as a language for precise reasoning.
description: Build a connected understanding of regular languages, grammars, Turing machines and formal logic. Original stories and worked examples turn definitions into tools for constructing models, testing claims and explaining impossibility.
coverage: An independently written guide to finite automata, grammars, computability and logic. Each topic includes original worked problems, definitions, reasoning checks and teaching notes.
prerequisites: Sets, functions and elementary proof by contradiction
Basic Python control flow and recursion
Comfort reading finite graphs and mathematical notation
outcomes: Construct and compare regular expressions, DFAs and NFAs
Design grammars and trace CNF conversion and CYK parsing
Separate decidability, recognizability and computational efficiency
Use truth assignments and quantifiers to assess formal claims

topics.title: Strings, languages and specifications
topics.story:
Imagine a gatekeeper checking delivery labels. Before choosing a scanner, the depot must say which labels are allowed: perhaps any sequence of A and B that ends in B. A specification describes that rule independently of the device used to check it. The device might keep a tiny light on its panel, run a program, or consult a lookup table.

Those implementations can look completely different yet make the same decisions. The analogy has a limit: real scanners can fail mechanically, whereas our mathematical machines follow their rules exactly. We study whether the rules describe the intended set of labels.
topics.principle:
An alphabet is a finite set of symbols; a string is a finite sequence over that alphabet. The empty string ε has length zero. A language is any subset of all finite strings, not necessarily a spoken language or a set with a practical description. A decision problem can be represented as language membership: yes instances belong to the language.

A specification states the input domain and required answer, while an algorithm provides a procedure. An implementation is correct only if its behavior satisfies that specification on every allowed input. For general computation, also state whether termination is required; producing correct answers whenever a program happens to finish is weaker than always producing an answer.
topics.formula: Σ* = ⋃ₖ≥₀ Σᵏ;  L ⊆ Σ*;  |ε| = 0
topics.symbols:
Σ is the alphabet and Σᵏ is the set of strings of length k. The star means all finite lengths, including length zero, so ε always belongs to Σ*. L is a language chosen from that universe.

Vertical bars give string length here, not set size. These definitions describe allowable inputs and yes answers; they do not assert that a machine exists to decide membership in every possible L.
topics.example:
Take Σ = {A, B} and specify L as the strings ending in B. The strings B, AB and BAB belong; ε, A and BAA do not. A correct decision procedure first handles an empty input by rejecting, then checks whether the last symbol is B.

It may inspect the final character directly if the representation permits that, or scan left to right while remembering the latest character. Both procedures implement the same specification. A procedure that merely checks whether B occurs anywhere fails on BAA, providing a concrete counterexample rather than just an intuition that something is wrong.
topics.pitfall: Confusing ε with ∅: ε is one string; ∅ contains no strings. The language {ε} has one member.

check.question: Is the set of all binary strings a single string?
check.answer: No. It is the infinite language {0,1}*. Every individual member is finite, even though there are infinitely many members.

glossary.meaning: A finite set of allowed symbols.
A finite ordered sequence of symbols.
A rule stating allowed inputs and required outputs.

guided_questions.question: Why separate a rule from a scanner?
guided_questions.answer: Different procedures can satisfy the same rule; we must judge them against one shared target.

guided_questions.question: How many length-two strings use {x,y}?
guided_questions.answer: Each of two positions has two choices, giving 2×2=4: xx, xy, yx, yy.

guided_questions.question: Is {ε} empty?
guided_questions.answer: No. It contains one string of length zero.

instructor_notes.title: Input validity comes first
instructor_notes.body: If the alphabet is {x,y}, the string xz is outside the input domain. Decide whether an implementation reports an input error or a no answer; do not silently change the mathematical language.

instructor_notes.title: A counterexample is decisive
instructor_notes.body: One disagreement is enough to disprove an implementation’s universal correctness claim. A thousand successful tests do not cover infinitely many inputs.

worked_problems.title: Count a finite slice
worked_problems.question: Over Σ={x,y}, list every string of length at most two that ends in x. Count ε among candidate inputs, but apply the ending rule literally.
worked_problems.strategy: Partition by length so no candidate is missed or counted twice.
steps: Length zero contributes ε. It has no final x, so reject it.
Length one contributes x and y. Only x ends in x.
Length two contributes xx, xy, yx, yy. Inspecting the second position keeps xx and yx.
worked_problems.answer: The selected language slice is {x,xx,yx}, containing three strings.
worked_problems.sanity_check: For positive length n, fixing the final x leaves 2^(n−1) choices. At n=1 and 2 this gives 1+2=3.

worked_problems.title: Repair an incorrect test
worked_problems.question: The rule is “binary input contains exactly two 1s.” A proposed test accepts whenever length is two. Test 10 and 101, then state a correct procedure that halts.
worked_problems.strategy: Compare the proposed predicate with the actual count, then replace the predicate.
steps: For 10, length is two, so the proposal accepts. Its 1-count is one, so the required answer is no.
For 101, length is three, so the proposal rejects. Its 1-count is two, so the required answer is yes.
Scan the finite input once, adding one when a 1 appears. After the last symbol, accept exactly when the count equals two.
worked_problems.answer: The length-only test has both false acceptance and false rejection. The counting procedure halts after all input symbols.
worked_problems.sanity_check: The empty string gives count zero and is rejected, while 11 gives count two and is accepted.

topics.title: Regular expressions as language algebra
topics.story:
A small toy factory builds products from three instructions: choose one of two designs, place two pieces side by side, or repeat a piece any finite number of times. A regular expression is a similar recipe for strings. Choice produces alternatives, concatenation joins pieces, and repetition allows a variable number of copies.

The recipe describes all possible finished products, not the order in which a factory makes them. Repetition can choose zero copies, which is easy to miss. Also, this mathematical recipe excludes powerful extras found in some programming libraries, so claims about regular languages should use the basic operations explicitly.
topics.principle:
Regular expressions are built recursively from symbols, the empty language, the empty string, union, concatenation and Kleene star. Their semantics assign a language to every expression. Union accepts a string from either operand. Concatenation accepts strings that can be split into a left part from the first language and a right part from the second. Star permits zero or more concatenated members of one language.

Parentheses determine grouping; standard shorthand gives star higher precedence than concatenation, and concatenation higher precedence than union. Matching here means membership of the whole string. Substring search is a different task unless the expression explicitly permits arbitrary surrounding text. A regular expression is a specification, not a commitment to a particular backtracking implementation.
topics.symbols:
R and S denote expressions, while L(R) denotes the language represented by R. The vertical bar inside an expression denotes choice. The product uv is string concatenation, and the superscript k means k concatenated pieces rather than numerical exponentiation of a string.

In particular, L(R)⁰ is {ε}. These equations are recursive definitions: evaluate small expressions first, then combine their languages using the corresponding operation.
topics.example:
Consider R = (ab|c)*d over {a,b,c,d}. Each repeated block is either ab or c, followed by exactly one final d. Choosing the blocks ab, c, ab produces abcabd, which matches. Choosing zero blocks produces d, so that also matches.

The string acd fails: before the final d, the prefix ac cannot be divided into ab and c blocks because its first a lacks the required following b. The string dcc fails because the d must occur at the end. Writing out the block decomposition gives a direct membership explanation.
topics.pitfall: Assuming R* excludes the empty string. Zero repetitions always contribute ε, even when R itself matches nothing.

check.question: What is the difference between a*b and (ab)*?
check.answer: a*b has any number of a symbols followed by one b. (ab)* repeats an entire ab block and also includes ε; for example aab belongs only to the first.

glossary.meaning: Accept a string from either alternative.
Place one string after another.
Zero or more concatenated members of a language.

guided_questions.question: Why does zero repetition matter?
guided_questions.answer: It adds ε even if the repeated block is nonempty.

guided_questions.question: How can xyx be split for (xy|x)*?
guided_questions.answer: Choose xy followed by x, so it belongs.

guided_questions.question: Does matching a prefix prove a whole match?
guided_questions.answer: No. Every remaining symbol must also be consumed by the expression.

instructor_notes.title: Expression versus implementation
instructor_notes.body: The expression says which strings belong. Backtracking and simultaneous state simulation may execute it differently while agreeing on all answers.

instructor_notes.title: Star is not plus
instructor_notes.body: One-or-more repetition can be written RR*. Its omission of ε matters when R itself cannot generate ε.

worked_problems.title: Decompose a new pattern
worked_problems.question: For R=(xy|z)*x, decide membership of xyzzx, x and zxy. Match the whole string.
worked_problems.strategy: Separate the final required x before decomposing the repeated prefix.
steps: xyzzx ends with x. The prefix xyzz splits as xy,z,z, all allowed blocks.
The string x leaves an empty prefix. Zero repeated blocks are allowed by star.
zxy ends in y, so it cannot supply the final x, regardless of its earlier blocks.
worked_problems.answer: xyzzx and x match; zxy does not.
worked_problems.sanity_check: Removing the final x from the pattern would change the language: ε would then match.

worked_problems.title: Compare star placement
worked_problems.question: Over {a,b}, find a string in a*b* but not (ab)*, and a string in (ab)* but not a*b*.
worked_problems.strategy: Inspect block order: grouped runs versus alternating pairs.
steps: The string aab has two a symbols followed by one b, so it belongs to a*b*.
Every nonempty (ab)* string alternates a then b and has even length. aab has length three, so it is excluded.
The string abab is two ab blocks, but after its first b another a occurs. This violates the all-a-before-all-b structure.
worked_problems.answer: aab witnesses the first difference; abab witnesses the reverse. Neither language contains the other.
worked_problems.sanity_check: Both expressions still accept ε, so sharing the empty string does not establish equivalence.

topics.title: DFA states as summaries of the past
topics.story:
A doorway counter needs only two lights to report whether an even or odd number of people has entered. It does not retain every arrival time. Each new arrival toggles the light, and the current light summarizes everything relevant to the final parity question.

A deterministic finite automaton uses states in this way: each state represents an information summary of the prefix already read. A good design begins by naming what each state means. The analogy stops when a task requires an unbounded exact count, because a fixed number of lights cannot remember arbitrarily many distinct totals.
topics.principle:
A DFA has a finite state set, an input alphabet, one start state, a set of accepting states and a total transition function. It processes exactly one symbol per transition. Every input therefore has one run, and acceptance depends on the state reached after the entire input has been consumed. Design states around an invariant: after reading a prefix, what information does the current state certify?

For parity, only even versus odd matters. For a fixed substring, a state can summarize the longest useful suffix. A complete definition includes every state-symbol transition, even transitions to a rejecting sink. Correctness follows by showing that the invariant holds initially and survives each transition, then relating accepting states to the specification.
topics.formula:
D = (Q, Σ, δ, q₀, F)
δ : Q × Σ → Q
w ∈ L(D) ⇔ δ*(q₀,w) ∈ F
topics.symbols:
Q is the finite set of states; q₀ is its start state and F is its accepting subset. δ gives the next state for one symbol. δ* extends this operation to a whole string: start at q₀ and apply δ repeatedly, with δ*(q,ε)=q.

The star on δ means an extended transition function here, rather than language repetition. The acceptance condition is checked only after all input symbols have been read.
topics.example:
Build a DFA for binary strings containing an odd number of 1 symbols. Use states E and O, start at E, and accept only O. Reading 0 leaves either state unchanged. Reading 1 toggles E to O or O to E. On 10110 the state sequence is E, O, O, E, O, O, so the input is accepted.

On ε the state stays E, giving rejection. The invariant is precise: E means the processed prefix has even 1-count, and O means odd 1-count. That invariant proves the rule for every string, not just the examples.
topics.pitfall: Accepting as soon as an accepting state is visited. A later symbol may leave that state; the whole input must be consumed.

check.question: How many states suffice to recognize binary strings with a number of 1s divisible by three?
check.answer: Three states, representing the count modulo three. Reading 1 advances the residue; reading 0 leaves it unchanged. Only residue zero accepts.

glossary.meaning: A finite summary of the processed prefix.
A statement preserved after every transition.
A state that accepts if input has ended there.

guided_questions.question: Why does a modulo counter need few states?
guided_questions.answer: The question ignores complete totals and only needs a remainder.

guided_questions.question: What happens to remainder two after another 1 modulo three?
guided_questions.answer: 2+1=3 has remainder zero, so transition to state zero.

guided_questions.question: Does an accepting prefix ensure an accepted extension?
guided_questions.answer: No. An additional symbol can change the summarized property.

instructor_notes.title: Prove what the state means
instructor_notes.body: For a remainder machine, initialization uses count zero. A 0 preserves count; a 1 raises count and remainder together. These two cases prove every transition, not just one run.

instructor_notes.title: Representation is a design choice
instructor_notes.body: To ask whether the last symbol is 1, parity states are insufficient: 10 and 1 have the same parity but different last symbols. Choose the summary for the actual question.

worked_problems.title: Trace a remainder machine
worked_problems.question: Use states 0,1,2 for number of 1s modulo three. Start and accept at 0; reading 0 stays, reading 1 adds one modulo three. Trace 110101.
worked_problems.strategy: Record one state after each symbol and check the invariant against the cumulative count.
steps: Start with count zero and state 0. The first two 1s give counts 1,2 and states 1,2.
The next 0 leaves state 2. The next 1 raises count to three and returns state to 0.
The final 0 leaves state 0; the final 1 raises count to four and ends in state 1.
worked_problems.answer: The full state trace is 0,1,2,2,0,0,1. Reject because four is not divisible by three.
worked_problems.sanity_check: Directly count four 1s: 4 mod 3=1, independently matching the final state.

worked_problems.title: Design a last-symbol machine
worked_problems.question: Over {a,b}, design a complete DFA accepting nonempty strings ending in b. Use only two states.
worked_problems.strategy: Remember only whether the most recently read symbol is b; group the empty prefix with rejection.
steps: Name states N and B. N means empty or last symbol a; B means last symbol b. Start at N.
From either state, reading a goes to N and reading b goes to B. This specifies all four state-symbol pairs.
Accept only B after input ends. On bab the states are N,B,N,B; on ε the state stays N.
worked_problems.answer: This complete DFA accepts bab and rejects ε, exactly following the final-symbol rule.
worked_problems.sanity_check: Appending a to any accepted string forces N, as the required final character has changed.

topics.title: Nondeterminism and epsilon moves
topics.story:
Suppose a team searches a maze with a printed sequence of colored doors. At a junction, the team can explore every compatible branch. The mission succeeds when at least one explorer follows the entire color sequence and finishes in an approved room. A failed branch does not cancel a successful one.

Some corridors are uncolored and can be crossed without consuming a color from the list. Those resemble epsilon transitions. This is a reasoning device, not a claim that computers own infinitely many physical explorers: a finite set of reachable states can represent all active branches at once.
topics.principle:
An NFA allows zero, one or several next states for a state-symbol pair. An epsilon transition changes state without reading a symbol. Acceptance is existential: some finite path must consume the entire input and end in an accepting state. Paths that get stuck, finish in nonaccepting states or loop on epsilon moves do not invalidate another successful path.

NFAs are often easier to compose than DFAs. Union chooses a branch, concatenation links an accepting point of one machine to the next, and star permits repeated traversal with an empty-input option. These constructions explain how to turn regular expressions into automata. Nondeterminism changes the convenience and size of a description, but it does not enlarge the family of regular languages.
topics.formula:
δ : Q × (Σ ∪ {ε}) → 𝒫(Q)
Accept w iff some path labeled w ends in F
topics.symbols:
𝒫(Q) is the power set of Q, so one transition returns a set of possible states. ε labels consume no input symbols. A path label is obtained by concatenating its ordinary symbol labels and ignoring epsilon labels.

F is the accepting-state set. “Some” is the essential quantifier: acceptance needs one successful run. A missing transition means the empty set of next states, not an instruction to wait for a later symbol.
topics.example:
To recognize strings over {a,b} ending in ab, let a start state loop on both letters. From that state an a can also lead to a second state, which takes b to a final state with no outgoing transitions.

On baab, one branch guesses the first a as the start of the suffix and then fails on the next a. Another branch waits, guesses the second a, then reads the final b and accepts. On aba, a branch reaches the final state after ab but cannot consume the last a, so the whole string is rejected.
topics.pitfall: Complementing an NFA by swapping final and nonfinal states. Existential acceptance prevents this simple trick; convert to a complete DFA first.

check.question: If one branch accepts and another loops forever on epsilon moves, is the input accepted?
check.answer: Yes. NFA acceptance asks whether an accepting finite run exists; the behavior of another branch does not remove it.

glossary.meaning: A transition may offer several possible next states.
A state change that consumes no input symbol.
One finite successful complete run suffices.

guided_questions.question: Why can one failing branch be ignored?
guided_questions.answer: Acceptance requires at least one success, not success on every branch.

guided_questions.question: Does ε consume a space character?
guided_questions.answer: No. It consumes nothing; a literal space would be an ordinary alphabet symbol.

guided_questions.question: Can reaching a final state early suffice?
guided_questions.answer: Only if a successful continuation consumes all remaining symbols.

instructor_notes.title: Simulate possibilities together
instructor_notes.body: Track a set of reachable states after each prefix. Two paths arriving at the same state with the same unread suffix have identical future options and can be merged.

instructor_notes.title: An ε cycle is finite in the closure
instructor_notes.body: Closure search marks visited states. A cycle p→q→p adds p and q once each, rather than demanding endlessly repeated traversal.

worked_problems.title: A free branch before a letter
worked_problems.question: States are s,p,f. Start s, accept only f. Edges: s—ε→p, s—a→s, p—b→f. No other edges exist. Decide aab and ba.
worked_problems.strategy: Maintain active states including all free ε moves before and after each symbol.
steps: The initial closure is {s,p}. Each a uses the loop at s and then restores p by ε, so after aa the set is still {s,p}.
The last b moves p to f, so aab ends with active set {f} and accepts.
For ba, b first produces {f}. No a leaves f, so the active set becomes ∅ after a and the input rejects.
worked_problems.answer: aab is accepted; ba is rejected. Being final after a prefix is not enough.
worked_problems.sanity_check: The successful strings are exactly a*b: any number of a symbols and one final b.

worked_problems.title: Why swapping NFA finals fails
worked_problems.question: NFA states s,f, alphabet {a}, start s, final set {f}. Edges s—a→s and s—a→f only. Compare input a before and after swapping finals to {s}.
worked_problems.strategy: List both complete runs; complement should reverse the overall answer, not each path independently.
steps: Originally, input a has runs ending at s and f. The run ending at f accepts, so the NFA accepts.
After swapping finals, those same runs still exist. Now the run ending at s accepts.
Thus both machines accept a. A true complement must reject a because the original accepted it.
worked_problems.answer: Swapping finals does not produce the complement for this NFA.
worked_problems.sanity_check: Determinizing gives one subset {s,f} after a. Flipping acceptance of that single subset correctly reverses the answer.

topics.title: Converting an NFA to a DFA
topics.story:
A control-room display can replace a team of maze explorers with a set of illuminated rooms. After each incoming color, it turns off the old lights and illuminates every room the team could now occupy. There is only one display configuration after a given prefix, even though many explorers may have followed different routes.

That configuration is a DFA state. Epsilon corridors require a little extra work: illuminate every room reachable for free before continuing. The display may have many possible configurations, because a set of a few rooms has exponentially many subsets, even if only a small fraction occur during real runs.
topics.principle:
Subset construction makes one DFA state for each reachable set of NFA states. Begin with the epsilon closure of the NFA start state. To read a symbol, take all corresponding symbol transitions from the current set, then take epsilon closure again.

A subset is accepting when it intersects the NFA accepting set. The empty subset is a rejecting sink and should be included when it is reachable. The correctness invariant says that after every prefix, the DFA state equals exactly the states reachable in the NFA after that prefix, allowing epsilon moves.

This proves equal languages. A machine with m NFA states has at most 2ᵐ subset states, although an implementation should normally generate reachable subsets rather than enumerate all of them.
topics.formula:
S₀ = E({q₀})
Δ(S,a) = E(⋃q∈S δ(q,a))
S is accepting ⇔ S ∩ F ≠ ∅
topics.symbols:
E(S) is the epsilon closure of a state set S, including S itself and all states reachable using only epsilon edges. Δ is the transition function of the new DFA; δ belongs to the original NFA.

The union gathers every possible ordinary a move. F contains original accepting states. Read the final condition as “at least one active NFA state accepts,” which preserves the existential meaning of nondeterminism.
topics.example:
Take NFA states p, q and r. Start at p, allow an epsilon move p→q, let p loop on a, let q take b to r, and accept only r. The initial DFA state is {p,q}. Reading a moves p to p and q nowhere, then epsilon closure restores q, so the set remains {p,q}.

Reading b moves only q to r, producing {r}. A further a or b produces ∅. Therefore aab finishes in {r} and accepts, while aaba finishes in ∅ and rejects. The construction makes the language a*b visible without guessing individual paths.
topics.pitfall: Forgetting epsilon closure at the start or after a symbol. Either omission can lose a valid accepting path.

check.question: Can a subset containing both accepting and rejecting NFA states accept?
check.answer: Yes. It accepts whenever at least one contained state is accepting, because at least one NFA branch has succeeded.

glossary.meaning: One DFA state representing several possible NFA states.
All states reachable without consuming symbols, including the starting set.
A state whose every transition returns to itself.

guided_questions.question: Why close after each ordinary move?
guided_questions.answer: The NFA may then take free moves before reading another symbol.

guided_questions.question: How many subsets can four states have?
guided_questions.answer: Each state is either included or excluded, so 2⁴=16.

guided_questions.question: Must every possible subset be created?
guided_questions.answer: No. Reachable-subset construction omits those no input can reach.

instructor_notes.title: Closure contains its input
instructor_notes.body: A state can stay in place using zero ε moves. Forgetting that zero-step option can make a valid starting state disappear.

instructor_notes.title: The empty subset is useful
instructor_notes.body: Once no branch survives, no later symbol can revive one. The empty subset loops on every symbol and makes the resulting DFA complete.

worked_problems.title: Construct four reachable subsets
worked_problems.question: NFA states 0,1,2; start 0; final 2. Edges: 0—ε→1, 1—x→1, 1—y→2. Alphabet {x,y}; missing moves are empty. Build its reachable DFA.
worked_problems.strategy: Begin from the closure, then explore new subsets until none remain.
steps: Start A={0,1}. On x it reaches B={1}; on y it reaches C={2}.
B loops on x and goes to C on y. C has no ordinary moves, so both symbols reach D=∅.
D loops on both symbols. Only C contains final state 2, so only C accepts. Four subsets A,B,C,D are reachable.
worked_problems.answer: The DFA has four reachable subset states and recognizes x*y.
worked_problems.sanity_check: There are at most 2³=8 subsets. A and B behave identically and can later be merged, yielding a smaller equivalent DFA.

worked_problems.title: Close through a cycle
worked_problems.question: ε edges are p→q, q→r, r→q. The only a edge is r→f; only f is accepting. Start p. Find initial closure and the subset after a.
worked_problems.strategy: Use a visited set so a free-move cycle is explored finitely.
steps: Include p using zero moves. From p add q; from q add r.
From r the ε edge returns to q, already included. Stop with E({p})={p,q,r}.
On a, p and q contribute no destinations, while r contributes f. No ε leaves f, so the next subset is {f}.
worked_problems.answer: Initial subset is {p,q,r}; input a ends at accepting subset {f}.
worked_problems.sanity_check: Without the initial closure, p has no a move and the incorrect simulation would reject a.

topics.title: From automata back to expressions
topics.story:
Imagine redrawing a transport map after removing a small station. Every route that entered that station, possibly traveled around a local loop, and then left must be represented by a new direct connection. Existing direct routes remain available as alternatives. Repeating this process leaves only an origin and a destination, joined by a description of every possible journey.

State elimination performs that compression with regular expressions on edges. The final description can become much longer than the original map, and different station-removal orders can produce different-looking descriptions of exactly the same collection of journeys.
topics.principle:
A generalized NFA labels edges with regular expressions rather than single symbols. Add a fresh start state with no incoming edges and a fresh accepting state with no outgoing edges, connecting the old boundaries with epsilon edges.

Missing edges denote ∅, and parallel edges are combined by union. When removing a state k, update every surviving edge i→j with an alternative for traveling through k: enter it, loop there any number of times, then leave. Once only the new start and finish remain, their edge expression denotes the original language.

Together with expression-to-NFA and subset constructions, this establishes equal expressive power for regular expressions, NFAs and DFAs. Equal expressive power does not imply equal representation size or equal practical execution cost.
topics.formula: Rᵢⱼ ← Rᵢⱼ | Rᵢₖ(Rₖₖ)*Rₖⱼ
topics.symbols:
Rᵢⱼ denotes the expression labeling the current edge from state i to state j. State k is the one being removed. The new alternative concatenates an entry route, zero or more loops at k, and an exit route.

The old direct route stays in the union. All edge expressions used for one elimination step refer to the graph before that step; the formula applies to surviving states i and j.
topics.example:
Suppose a generalized automaton has start s, middle k and finish f. Its labels are s→k:a, k→k:b, k→f:c and s→f:d. Removing k changes the s→f label to d|ab*c. The string abbbc follows the a entry, three b loops and c exit.

The string ac uses zero loops, and d uses the original direct edge. The string abcabc is excluded because after reaching f there is no way to restart. If the direct edge had been absent, its label would be ∅ and the resulting expression would simplify to ab*c.
topics.pitfall: Dropping the old i→j expression when eliminating k. Routes that never visit k must remain represented.

check.question: What happens when the removed state has no self-loop?
check.answer: Its loop label is ∅, and ∅*={ε}. The new route is simply the entry expression followed by the exit expression.

glossary.meaning: An edge labelled by a regular expression.
Removing a state while preserving all possible surviving routes.
A route from a state back to itself.

guided_questions.question: Why keep the old edge?
guided_questions.answer: Some accepted routes never visit the removed state.

guided_questions.question: What does a missing loop contribute?
guided_questions.answer: Its star contributes ε, representing zero visits around the loop.

guided_questions.question: Does a longer expression mean a different language?
guided_questions.answer: No. Elimination order affects representation length without changing accepted strings.

instructor_notes.title: Use one old graph per update
instructor_notes.body: Compute every route through k from the pre-elimination labels. Mixing newly updated labels into the same step can accidentally count routes with unintended repeated structure.

instructor_notes.title: Empty language is an annihilator
instructor_notes.body: If there is no entry or no exit, that through-route is ∅. In contrast, an ε entry or exit costs no symbol but still permits the route.

worked_problems.title: Eliminate a looping middle state
worked_problems.question: States s,k,f have labels s→f:u, s→k:v, k→k:w|x, k→f:y. No other edges. Remove k and test vwxwy.
worked_problems.strategy: Separate routes that avoid k from those entering, looping and leaving it.
steps: The route avoiding k already contributes u and must remain.
The route through k contributes v(w|x)*y, since each loop independently chooses w or x.
For vwxwy, take entry v, loops w,x,w, and exit y. All pieces match the required order.
worked_problems.answer: The final expression is u|v(w|x)*y, and vwxwy is accepted.
worked_problems.sanity_check: The zero-loop path vy also matches; u remains accepted without entering k.

worked_problems.title: Distinguish no edge from a free edge
worked_problems.question: There is no s→f edge. Labels are s→k:ε, k→f:ab, and no k loop. Remove k. Then compare with the variant where s→k is absent.
worked_problems.strategy: Substitute ∅ for missing edges, but ε for existing free edges.
steps: In the first graph, substitute ∅ | ε(∅)*ab. The old direct alternative is empty.
Because ∅*={ε}, concatenate ε, ε and ab to obtain ab.
In the variant, entry is ∅, so ∅ | ∅(∅)*ab = ∅. No route can enter k.
worked_problems.answer: A free entry permits exactly ab; a missing entry permits no string.
worked_problems.sanity_check: Neither first graph nor its expression accepts ε, because the exit still requires both a and b.

topics.title: Matching strategy and repeated work
topics.story:
A librarian tries to divide a long row of identical cards into packets of one or two. If a final requirement cannot be met, the librarian might undo the latest choice and try another partition, then another, repeatedly exploring arrangements with the same remaining task. A more organized librarian records every distinct situation already reached and merges equivalent attempts.

This distinction explains why a compact regular expression can run slowly in a backtracking engine even though finite-state matching is possible. The pattern's mathematical language and the engine's search strategy are separate layers, and both matter when judging performance.
topics.principle:
The membership problem asks whether a whole input string belongs to a regular expression's language. A naive recursive or backtracking matcher can explore many decompositions of the same prefix, repeating equivalent subproblems. Thompson-style NFA simulation instead maintains a set of active states and updates that set per input symbol, including epsilon closure.

For an NFA with O(m) states and edges built from an expression of size m, straightforward active-state simulation takes O(mn) time on an input of length n and O(m) working space. Determinizing first permits O(n) matching for a fixed DFA with constant-time transitions, but constructing that DFA may require exponentially many states. These bounds concern basic regular expressions; extensions such as backreferences are outside this finite-state model.
topics.formula:
NFA simulation: O(mn) time, O(m) active-state space
Fixed DFA simulation: O(n) time, after preprocessing
topics.symbols:
m measures the size of a Thompson-style NFA, including its transitions, and n is input length. At each character, epsilon reachability and ordinary transitions are processed without endlessly revisiting already included states.

The DFA bound treats the automaton as already constructed and transition lookup as constant time. Neither bound says that every library engine implements this strategy, and preprocessing cost must be counted when the expression itself is part of the input.
topics.example:
Consider the expression (a|aa)*b and the string aaaaac. The five a symbols can be divided into blocks of one or two in several ways: a,a,a,a,a or aa,a,aa, among others. Every choice eventually fails because the required final b is absent. A backtracking strategy may rediscover that failure through many decompositions.

An NFA simulation merges branches that reach the same state after the same prefix, then rejects when c has no valid continuation. Appending b instead gives aaaaab, which matches. This example illustrates repeated search work without changing the regular language being specified.
topics.pitfall: Concluding that regular-expression matching is inherently exponential because one backtracking implementation takes exponential time on a pattern.

check.question: Why can two NFA runs reaching the same state after the same prefix be merged?
check.answer: Their remaining possible behavior depends only on that state and the unread suffix. The distinct histories add no information needed for membership.

glossary.meaning: Undo a choice and try an alternative path.
All states reachable after the current input prefix.
Work performed before a particular input is matched.

guided_questions.question: Why can a short pattern be slow?
guided_questions.answer: Its execution may revisit many decompositions that lead to the same failure.

guided_questions.question: What information lets two attempts merge?
guided_questions.answer: The same automaton state and the same input position give the same remaining task.

guided_questions.question: Is DFA construction always cheap?
guided_questions.answer: No. A subset construction can create exponentially many states even when later matching is linear.

instructor_notes.title: Count states, not imaginary people
instructor_notes.body: An active set never needs multiple copies of the same state for membership. Path counts may grow while the set stays small; counting parses is a different problem.

instructor_notes.title: Amortize setup only when justified
instructor_notes.body: A fixed DFA reused for many strings can spread construction cost over them. For a new pattern on every request, excluding setup can give a misleading comparison.

worked_problems.title: Count repeated decompositions
worked_problems.question: For pattern (a|aa)*b and input aaaaac, count decompositions of the five a symbols into length-one or length-two blocks. Do not claim a count of all engine instructions.
worked_problems.strategy: Let F(n) count decompositions. Condition on whether the first block has length one or two.
steps: F(0)=1 for the empty decomposition and F(1)=1 for one single block.
For n≥2, F(n)=F(n−1)+F(n−2), because removing the first block leaves one of those lengths. Thus F(2)=2 and F(3)=3.
Continue: F(4)=3+2=5 and F(5)=5+3=8. Every decomposition still meets c rather than the required b.
worked_problems.answer: There are eight decompositions, all unsuccessful. This measures repeated alternatives, not a universal runtime.
worked_problems.sanity_check: Replacing c by b changes membership to yes without changing the eight possible a-block decompositions.

worked_problems.title: Separate preparation from matching
worked_problems.question: Assume an already built DFA makes one transition per symbol. Three inputs have lengths 4,7,9. Its construction took 30 abstract work units; each transition costs one. Find matching and total cost.
worked_problems.strategy: Sum the per-input scans, then add the one-time preparation cost once.
steps: The first input requires four transitions; the second requires seven. Their subtotal is 11.
Add the third input’s nine transitions to obtain 20 matching units.
Add construction cost 30 once, giving 50 total units for the three inputs.
worked_problems.answer: Matching costs 20 units; the complete batch costs 50. Linear scanning does not erase setup.
worked_problems.sanity_check: If every input used a new DFA with the same construction cost, setup would be 90 and total 110.

topics.title: Closure and decision procedures for regular languages
topics.story:
Two security sensors can be monitored by one panel that records both sensor modes. If the first has three modes and the second has four, the combined panel needs at most twelve pairs. A policy can approve a pair when both sensors approve, when either approves, or when they disagree.

This illustrates the product of two automata. The choice of accepting pairs expresses the policy while the transition structure stays the same. Inspecting which pairs are reachable can then answer whether a disagreement is possible at all, providing a finite procedure for comparing two apparently different specifications.
topics.principle:
Regular languages are closed under union, intersection and complement. For complete DFAs over a common alphabet, a product construction tracks a pair of states and updates both components on each input symbol. Choose final pairs according to the desired Boolean operation. Complement is simpler: swap accepting and nonaccepting states of a complete DFA. Membership is decided by simulation.

Nonemptiness is decided by graph reachability from the start to an accepting state. Equivalence reduces to emptiness of the symmetric difference: if no reachable product state has exactly one accepting component, the machines agree on every string. Converting regular expressions to DFAs therefore gives decision procedures for expression equivalence, although the conversion may cause exponential growth.
topics.formula:
δ×((p,q),a) = (δ₁(p,a),δ₂(q,a))
L₁ = L₂ ⇔ (L₁ ∖ L₂) ∪ (L₂ ∖ L₁) = ∅
topics.symbols:
p and q are states of the first and second DFA, and δ₁ and δ₂ are their transition functions. δ× is the product transition. L₁ and L₂ denote the two languages.

Set difference keeps strings in one language but not the other; their union here is the symmetric difference. These formulas assume the same input alphabet. If needed, complete either automaton with a rejecting sink before taking complements or products.
topics.example:
Let machine A accept binary strings ending in 1, and machine B accept binary strings with an odd number of 1s. To compare them, start their product at (not-ending-in-1, even). On input 10, A first moves to its accepting state and then back to rejection; B toggles to odd on 1 and stays odd on 0.

The final pair has exactly one accepting component. Thus 10 witnesses that the languages differ. A reachability search can discover such a pair and reconstruct its input using predecessor links. One counterexample is sufficient; checking many agreeing strings is not.
topics.pitfall: Flipping final states in an incomplete DFA without adding a sink. Missing transitions must become accepting rejection-complement behavior too.

check.question: How can a finite search establish agreement on infinitely many strings?
check.answer: Every string induces a path in the finite product graph. If no reachable state represents disagreement, no string can be a counterexample.

glossary.meaning: A pair recording one state of each machine.
Strings belonging to exactly one of two languages.
Whether a finite path leads from the start to a state.

guided_questions.question: Why is one disagreement enough?
guided_questions.answer: Equivalence requires agreement on every input, so any counterexample defeats it.

guided_questions.question: What is the product size bound for three and five states?
guided_questions.answer: At most 3×5=15 pairs, though some can be unreachable.

guided_questions.question: Can swapping finals work on a complete DFA?
guided_questions.answer: Yes. Every input has exactly one complete run, so flipping its final acceptance flips the answer.

guided_questions.question: Why is testing many example words weaker than searching the product graph?
guided_questions.answer: A finite sample can miss a longer witness. The product graph covers every possible state pair reached by any word, despite having finitely many nodes.

instructor_notes.title: Common alphabet matters
instructor_notes.body: A complement is relative to Σ*. Changing the alphabet changes which unseen symbols must be rejected or accepted, so complete both machines over the same alphabet.

instructor_notes.title: Shortest evidence by breadth first
instructor_notes.body: Breadth-first search of the product finds a shortest disagreement word when each edge consumes one symbol. Store incoming symbols as well as parents to reconstruct it.

worked_problems.title: Intersect two small rules
worked_problems.question: Over {0,1}, A accepts even length and B accepts strings ending in 1. Construct the acceptance rule of the product and test 101 and 01.
worked_problems.strategy: Track length parity and final-symbol status independently; intersection needs both.
steps: Use product states (E,N),(E,Y),(O,N),(O,Y), starting at (E,N). Every symbol toggles parity; its value sets Y for 1 or N for 0.
101 has length three and ends in 1, so its state is (O,Y), which fails the even-length condition.
01 has length two and ends in 1, so it ends at (E,Y), the sole accepting pair.
worked_problems.answer: The intersection accepts 01 and rejects 101; only (E,Y) is final.
worked_problems.sanity_check: ε has even length but no last 1, so the chosen start pair correctly rejects it.

worked_problems.title: Find a language counterexample
worked_problems.question: A accepts an even number of 1s. B accepts strings ending in 0, with ε rejected. Over {0,1}, find a shortest disagreement including the possibility ε.
worked_problems.strategy: Check the start pair before exploring edges; an empty word has length zero.
steps: At ε, A has seen zero 1s. Zero is even, so A accepts.
B explicitly rejects ε because it has no last symbol. Thus the start pair already disagrees.
No string has length below zero, so no shorter disagreement is possible.
worked_problems.answer: ε is a shortest counterexample, and the languages differ immediately at their start states.
worked_problems.sanity_check: The string 0 is accepted by both, showing why starting only with nonempty examples could hide the easiest witness.

worked_problems.title: Trace the word aba in two machines
worked_problems.question: Compare contains-ab with ends-in-ab. Both machines start at 0 and accept only state 2. Use the transition tables in the program.
worked_problems.strategy: Track the pair after each letter and compare acceptance only after the complete word.
steps: Start at (0,0). After a, both reach state 1, giving (1,1).
After b, the pair is (2,2). The prefix ab is accepted by both.
After the final a, the pair is (2,1). Only contains-ab accepts.
worked_problems.answer: aba belongs to the symmetric difference, so the languages are not equal.
worked_problems.sanity_check: The only words of length below 3 that contain ab are ab itself; it also ends in ab. Thus no shorter witness exists.

code_examples.title: Find a shortest word that separates two DFAs
code_examples.intro: Two students build text filters. One accepts words containing ab anywhere. The other accepts words ending in ab. Their tests on ab and aab both pass, so they think the filters agree. Mina stops guessing test words. She runs both machines together and searches for a pair of states where exactly one accepts. The search returns aba, a concrete explanation of the disagreement.
code_examples.output:
shortest witness: 'aba'
contains ab: True
ends in ab: False
walkthrough: A product state (x,y) records where both machines are after the same input prefix.
Mark a pair as visited when enqueuing it. The graph has at most |Q_A|*|Q_B| pairs.
Accept a product state when exactly one component accepts. This is symmetric difference, not intersection.
Use parent pointers to recover the word. BFS makes the first witness shortest in number of symbols.
code_examples.explanation:
Two languages differ exactly when their symmetric difference is nonempty: L(A) != L(B) iff there exists w with accept_A(w) XOR accept_B(w). A complete product search decides this condition for the supplied finite machines. If no mismatching pair is reachable, every word leads to an agreeing pair.

With q_A and q_B states and alphabet size s, time is O(s*q_A*q_B) and stored states use O(q_A*q_B). Completeness matters: every state needs a transition for each alphabet symbol. Missing transitions should first be sent to an explicit rejecting sink.

A returned empty string is a valid witness if the start states disagree. None means no witness exists. The small brute-force check verifies that no shorter word works for this fixture, but the visited-product argument explains why the general search terminates. This method compares DFAs; it is not a general equivalence test for arbitrary programs.

topics.title: Proving that finite memory is insufficient
topics.story:
A cloakroom attendant has a fixed set of cards to remember how many guests have entered. If the attendant must later admit exactly the same number of exits, eventually two different arrival totals must share a card. From that moment, identical exit sequences produce identical behavior even though one total should pass and the other should fail.

This is more than a failed attempt to invent better cards: it is an argument against every fixed finite card system. The crucial issue is an unbounded exact requirement. A bounded maximum number of guests, or merely counting modulo a fixed number, changes the problem.
topics.principle:
To prove a language nonregular, show that no finite-state summary can preserve all distinctions needed by future suffixes. For L={aⁿbⁿ:n≥0}, assume a DFA with m states exists. Among the m+1 prefixes ε,a,…,aᵐ, two different prefixes aⁱ and aʲ must lead to the same state. Appending the same suffix bⁱ then makes the machine behave identically on both strings.

But aⁱbⁱ belongs to L and aʲbⁱ does not. This contradiction proves nonregularity. Another technique uses closure: if a hypothetical regular language combined with known regular languages would produce a known nonregular one, the hypothesis fails. Neither argument says that the language is undecidable; it only rules out finite automata.
topics.formula:
δ*(q₀,aⁱ) = δ*(q₀,aʲ), i < j
⇒ δ*(q₀,aⁱbⁱ) = δ*(q₀,aʲbⁱ)
topics.symbols:
m is the number of states, so m+1 examined prefixes force a repeated state by the pigeonhole principle. i and j are two distinct prefix lengths, and bⁱ is a shared distinguishing suffix. δ* is the extended DFA transition.

The implication follows because a deterministic machine in the same state processes the same remaining input identically. The contradiction concerns membership of the two completed strings, not their different lengths alone.
topics.example:
Consider the language E of strings over {a,b} with equally many a and b symbols in any order. Suppose E were regular. The language a*b* is regular, and regular languages are closed under intersection. Their intersection would contain exactly a block of a symbols followed by an equally long block of b symbols: {aⁿbⁿ:n≥0}.

The repeated-state argument proves that language nonregular, giving a contradiction. Therefore E is not regular either. Notice that abba belongs to E but not to a*b*; the intersection deliberately removes mixed-order strings to expose the known hard pattern.
topics.pitfall: Claiming that failure to draw a DFA proves nonregularity. A proof must rule out every possible finite DFA, not only designs tried so far.

check.question: Is {aⁿbⁿ:0≤n≤20} nonregular?
check.answer: No. It is finite, so a DFA or a finite union of explicit expressions can recognize it. The unbounded requirement drives the impossibility proof.

glossary.meaning: More objects than categories force two objects into one category.
The same appended string creates different required membership answers.
No finite automaton recognizes the language.

guided_questions.question: Why use m+1 prefixes?
guided_questions.answer: There are only m states, so some two prefixes must share one.

guided_questions.question: Why append exactly bⁱ?
guided_questions.answer: It balances the shorter a-prefix but not the longer one.

guided_questions.question: Does nonregular mean no algorithm can decide it?
guided_questions.answer: No. A machine with unbounded working memory can count and compare these finite inputs.

instructor_notes.title: Quantifiers carry the proof
instructor_notes.body: The state count m is arbitrary. Showing one three-state machine fails would be weaker than starting from any finite m and deriving a contradiction.

instructor_notes.title: A bound changes the language
instructor_notes.body: Restricting n≤3 leaves only ε,ab,aabb,aaabbb. A finite list can always be recognized, even though the unbounded pattern cannot use finite memory.

worked_problems.title: Work through a forced collision
worked_problems.question: Suppose a hypothetical DFA for {aⁿbⁿ:n≥0} reaches the same state after a² and a⁵. Explain why this collision contradicts correctness.
worked_problems.strategy: Find one common suffix that one prefix needs and the other must reject.
steps: Choose suffix b² because it supplies exactly two b symbols for the shorter prefix.
The completed a²b² has equal counts and must be accepted; a⁵b² has five a and two b and must be rejected.
Both runs start that suffix in the same state. Determinism forces identical later states and final decisions, contradicting those requirements.
worked_problems.answer: Those two prefixes cannot share a state in any correct DFA for the language. Arbitrarily many needed distinctions rule out a finite DFA.
worked_problems.sanity_check: Using suffix b⁵ reverses which completed string is balanced and yields the same contradiction.

worked_problems.title: A bounded version is regular
worked_problems.question: Let L₃={aⁿbⁿ:0≤n≤3}. Give a regular expression and explain why the infinite-language proof does not apply unchanged.
worked_problems.strategy: Enumerate the finitely many allowed n values rather than seek a repeated unbounded counter.
steps: n=0 gives ε and n=1 gives ab.
n=2 gives aabb and n=3 gives aaabbb; there are no other allowed n values.
Take the union ε|ab|aabb|aaabbb. A finite expression is a regular description of all four strings.
worked_problems.answer: L₃ is regular. The earlier proof needs arbitrarily many distinct necessary prefixes, absent under this fixed bound.
worked_problems.sanity_check: a⁴b⁴ is rejected despite having equal counts, because n=4 exceeds the stated limit.

topics.title: Grammars and recursive structure
topics.story:
A builder can make a nested storage box by choosing either an empty compartment or a small box enclosed inside a larger one. The instructions can refer back to themselves, so a finite recipe produces arbitrarily deep nesting. A context-free grammar works similarly: a named unfinished component can be replaced with a pattern containing terminals and more unfinished components.

The final object is complete only when no unfinished components remain. This analogy explains recursion, but a grammar does not prescribe a physical execution schedule. Different replacement orders may describe the same structure and produce the same final string.
topics.principle:
A CFG consists of nonterminal variables, terminal symbols, production rules and a start variable. Each rule replaces one nonterminal with a finite sequence, possibly ε. “Context-free” means the rule is available regardless of neighboring symbols. A derivation begins at the start variable; only all-terminal results belong to the language.

Grammars express nesting beyond finite-state memory. Correctness has two directions: every generated string must satisfy the intended property, and every intended string must be generatable.

Context-free languages are closed under union, concatenation and star: rename component variables to avoid collisions, then add a fresh start rule choosing, joining or repeating their start variables. Unlike regular languages, they are not closed under arbitrary intersection or complement. Every regular language is context-free, but the reverse is false.
topics.formula:
G = (V, Σ, P, S)
L(G) = {w ∈ Σ* : S ⇒* w}
topics.symbols:
V is the set of nonterminals, Σ the disjoint terminal alphabet, P the production set and S the start nonterminal. One ⇒ means one rewriting step; ⇒* means zero or more such steps.

A derivation may pass through mixed strings containing nonterminals, but these intermediate forms are not language members. The condition w∈Σ* ensures that the final result contains only terminals, including the possible empty string ε.
topics.example:
Use the grammar S→[S]S | ε for balanced square brackets. To generate [][] first choose S⇒[S]S, replace the inner S by ε to obtain []S, expand the remaining S to [S]S, and replace both remaining variables by ε. To generate [[]], expand the first inner S instead.

Why does this grammar cover every balanced bracket string? Any nonempty balanced string has an initial [ whose matching ] separates an interior balanced string from a following balanced suffix. Those two smaller pieces fit exactly the two S positions. This decomposition supports a proof by induction on string length.
topics.pitfall: Mistaking a sentential form such as [S] for a generated terminal string. A derivation must finish all nonterminals.

check.question: What language does S→aS | b generate?
check.answer: Exactly {aⁿb:n≥0}. Each recursive step adds one leading a; the final rule contributes one b and ends the derivation.

glossary.meaning: A named component that still needs rewriting.
A symbol allowed in the finished string.
A sequence of rule applications starting at the start variable.

guided_questions.question: Why can a finite grammar generate infinitely many strings?
guided_questions.answer: A recursive rule can be applied any finite number of times.

guided_questions.question: Is aSb already a language member?
guided_questions.answer: Not while S is a nonterminal; its remaining work must be finished.

guided_questions.question: Does generating several examples prove completeness?
guided_questions.answer: No. One must explain how every intended string can be generated.

instructor_notes.title: Soundness and completeness differ
instructor_notes.body: A grammar that generates only ε is sound for balanced brackets but incomplete. It never generates a bad bracket string, yet misses every nonempty good one.

instructor_notes.title: Rename before combining
instructor_notes.body: Two grammars may both call a variable S while meaning different things. Rename their variables before joining them; otherwise rules can interact unintentionally.

worked_problems.title: Generate a mirrored word
worked_problems.question: Grammar S→aSa|bSb|ε over {a,b}. Give a complete derivation of abba and describe a property of every generated word.
worked_problems.strategy: Match the outer equal symbols, recurse on the middle, and stop with ε.
steps: The outer symbols of abba are a, so apply S⇒aSa.
Its inner target is bb, so replace that S using bSb: aSa⇒abSba.
Replace the remaining S by ε, obtaining abba with no variables left. Each wrapping adds two equal end symbols.
worked_problems.answer: S⇒aSa⇒abSba⇒abba. Every generated word is an even-length palindrome.
worked_problems.sanity_check: The word aba is a palindrome but odd length, so this grammar cannot generate it. The length invariant explains why.

worked_problems.title: Build concatenation with fresh names
worked_problems.question: G₁ has A→aA|ε and G₂ has B→bB|b. Build a grammar for one G₁ string followed by one G₂ string, then derive aab.
worked_problems.strategy: Keep disjoint variables A and B and use a fresh start that joins them.
steps: Add S→AB. A generates zero or more a symbols and B generates one or more b symbols.
Derive S⇒AB⇒aAB⇒aaAB⇒aaB by two recursive A steps and then A→ε.
Use B→b to obtain aab. No rule can place an a after a b because the two components remain in order.
worked_problems.answer: The grammar generates a*b⁺, meaning any a block followed by a nonempty b block. It derives aab.
worked_problems.sanity_check: b is allowed when A disappears immediately, while ε is excluded because B cannot vanish.

topics.title: Parse trees and ambiguity
topics.story:
A written expression can resemble a set of assembly instructions with missing grouping marks. If one technician joins the first two pieces before adding the third, while another joins the last two first, they may build different structures from the same line of symbols. A parse tree makes the structure explicit.

Its leaves record the visible string, while its internal nodes show how the grammar assembled it. Two different schedules of doing independent work do not necessarily create different structures. Ambiguity is about different trees, so it cannot be established merely by listing two arbitrary orders of applying rules.
topics.principle:
A parse tree records one derivation's hierarchical structure. Its root is the start variable, each internal node expands according to a production, and the leaf yield is read left to right. A grammar is ambiguous when some string has two distinct parse trees, equivalently two distinct leftmost derivations.

Arithmetic grammars such as E→E+E | E×E | n are ambiguous because neither operator precedence nor associativity is fixed. A layered grammar can enforce precedence: expressions combine terms by addition, terms combine factors by multiplication, and factors provide atoms or parentheses.

Ambiguity belongs to a particular grammar; demonstrating one ambiguous grammar does not prove that its language has no unambiguous grammar. Parsing chooses structure, which is necessary before evaluation or translation can be reliable.
topics.formula: Ambiguous G ⇔ ∃w ∈ L(G) with at least two distinct parse trees
topics.symbols:
G is a grammar and w is a terminal string. The existential quantifier means one witness string is enough. Distinct parse trees differ in their production structure, not in handwriting or traversal order.

A leftmost derivation always expands the leftmost remaining nonterminal, removing irrelevant choices of expansion schedule. The statement is a definition of ambiguity rather than an algorithm that decides ambiguity for every possible grammar.
topics.example:
For E→E+E | E×E | n, the string n+n×n has one tree whose root operation is addition and another whose root is multiplication. Assigning the three n leaves values 2, 3 and 4 gives 2+(3×4)=14 under the first tree, but (2+3)×4=20 under the second.

To enforce multiplication precedence, use E→E+T | T, T→T×F | F and F→n | (E). Now an unparenthesized multiplication is built inside a term, so the addition must sit above it. Parentheses can still request the other interpretation explicitly.
topics.pitfall: Calling two derivations ambiguous when they only expand independent branches in different orders. Compare trees or use leftmost derivations.

check.question: Can an ambiguous grammar generate a regular language?
check.answer: Yes. Ambiguity concerns the representation, not its expressive class. For example S→A|B, A→a and B→a gives two parses of the finite regular language {a}.

glossary.meaning: A hierarchy showing which grammar rules build the string.
A rule deciding which operator groups more tightly.
How repeated operators at the same level group.

guided_questions.question: Why are two arbitrary derivations insufficient?
guided_questions.answer: They might only expand independent branches in different orders and describe one tree.

guided_questions.question: How can one expression have values 17 and 27?
Does addition precedence also settle subtraction associativity?
guided_questions.answer: No. Repeated subtraction needs a separate grouping rule.

guided_questions.question: Why multiply inside one split but add across splits?
guided_questions.answer: Inside a split, each left tree can pair with every right tree. Across splits, a tree has exactly one root partition, so the sets are disjoint.

instructor_notes.title: Same value can hide ambiguity
instructor_notes.body: Two trees for 1+2+3 both evaluate to six, but they remain distinct trees. Equality of numeric results does not prove a grammar unambiguous.

instructor_notes.title: Repair the grammar rather than guess
instructor_notes.body: Separating expression, term and factor makes precedence part of syntax. An evaluator can then follow the tree instead of adding an inconsistent after-the-fact rule.

worked_problems.title: Two trees, different results
worked_problems.question: Use E→E+E|E×E|n, where n denotes a number token. The three number tokens display values 5, 4 and 3 in that order. Exhibit two parses of 5+4×3 and evaluate them.
worked_problems.strategy: Choose a different root operation while keeping the leaf sequence unchanged.
steps: Choose root +, with left leaf 5 and right subtree 4×3. Multiply first: 4×3=12.
Add at the root: 5+12=17. This tree represents 5+(4×3).
Choose root × instead, with left subtree 5+4=9 and right leaf 3. Its root value is 9×3=27.
worked_problems.answer: Both trees yield the same unparenthesized text but values 17 and 27, proving this grammar ambiguous.
worked_problems.sanity_check: Adding explicit parentheses distinguishes the two requested structures and removes this particular ambiguity.

worked_problems.title: Expansion order is not tree ambiguity
worked_problems.question: Grammar S→AB, A→a, B→b has no other productions. Compare expanding A first versus B first.
worked_problems.strategy: Write both derivations, then compare their parent–child structure.
steps: Expanding A first gives S⇒AB⇒aB⇒ab.
Expanding B first gives S⇒AB⇒Ab⇒ab.
Both trees have root S, children A and B, and leaves a under A and b under B. No production choice differs.
worked_problems.answer: The two schedules describe one parse tree. They do not establish ambiguity; this grammar is unambiguous.
worked_problems.sanity_check: Only the first schedule is leftmost throughout, which removes the irrelevant order choice.

worked_problems.title: Calculate five trees from smaller cases
worked_problems.question: For E -> E+E | n, calculate T(4) without listing all derivation orders.
worked_problems.strategy: Count tree structures by the root split. Different orders of expanding nodes can produce the same tree and must not be counted twice.
worked_problems.answer: There are five parse trees. The program prints all five distinct parenthesizations.
worked_problems.sanity_check: With three operands, the two trees are ((n+n)+n) and (n+(n+n)). This confirms the first nontrivial case.

code_examples.title: Count parse trees instead of assuming one
code_examples.intro: A calculator accepts n+n+n+n. Mina draws a tree by joining the first pair, but her friend joins the final pair first. Both follow E -> E+E | n. The text is valid, yet its structure is not unique. Mina counts all root splits and then combines the possible left and right trees. She discovers five trees and understands why a parser needs an associativity rule.
walkthrough: With one operand, there is one leaf tree. This is the base case, not zero.
For a root split after left operands, multiply the counts of left and right trees. Each pair makes one tree.
Sum across distinct root splits. They cannot describe the same ordered tree because their root partitions differ.
Enumerate only four operands for display. Counting and materializing every tree have very different output costs.
code_examples.explanation:
Let T(m) count parse trees for m identical operand tokens separated by plus. T(1)=1 and T(m)=sum from k=1 to m-1 of T(k)*T(m-k). k is the number of leaves on the left. For m=4, the three root choices contribute 1*2, 1*1 and 2*1, giving 5.

The counter takes O(m²) arithmetic operations and O(m) stored integers. Large counts need large integers, so this operation-count model does not claim constant-cost arithmetic for arbitrarily large m. Enumerating every tree costs at least the number of characters printed and grows much faster.

Equal arithmetic results do not make a grammar unambiguous. Ambiguity is about multiple parse trees for the same token string. The grammar E -> E+n | n fixes left association for this simple language. This example assumes an already tokenized plus-only expression; it does not implement a lexer, precedence for other operators or a general grammar parser.

topics.title: Chomsky normal form without changing the language
topics.story:
A furniture company wants every assembly instruction to have one of two shapes: join two unfinished components, or attach one finished piece. Complex instructions are split into smaller named stages. Optional components and aliases need careful handling so that the revised booklet still builds exactly the same products.

Chomsky normal form provides this disciplined shape for grammar rules. The aim is not to make the instructions short or elegant; it is to make parsing easier to reason about. A special empty-product exception is preserved separately, because an assembly tree with visible leaves cannot represent a product containing no pieces.
topics.principle:
In CNF, ordinary productions have form A→BC or A→a. A fresh start symbol may additionally produce ε if the language contains it, and that start symbol must not occur on any right-hand side. Conversion preserves the language by introducing helper variables for terminals in longer rules, splitting long right-hand sides into binary rules, eliminating nullable-variable occurrences with all required alternatives, and removing unit productions through reachability among aliases.

The order and bookkeeping matter: a nullable variable may occur more than once, and deleting epsilon rules without adding alternatives loses strings. For a nonempty word of length n, a CNF parse has n terminal-producing nodes and n−1 binary-production nodes. This bounded shape makes membership decidable and supports dynamic programming.
topics.formula:
A→BC or A→a; optionally S₀→ε
Nonempty parse with n terminals uses 2n−1 production applications
topics.symbols:
A, B and C are nonterminals, a is a terminal and S₀ is the protected start symbol. The optional empty production is the only epsilon exception. n is the length of a nonempty derived string.

Its binary parse skeleton has n leaves and n−1 internal branching nodes; terminal productions add the n leaf applications. This count assumes CNF and does not apply to arbitrary grammars with unit chains or nullable cycles.
topics.example:
Start with S→aS | b. Introduce A→a so the mixed rule becomes S→AS. Because S appears on a right-hand side, introduce a new start S₀ and initially link S₀→S. Removing that unit rule copies S's nonunit productions, giving S₀→AS | b, S→AS | b and A→a.

The result is CNF and still generates aⁿb for n≥0. For aab, derive S₀⇒AS⇒aS⇒aAS⇒aaS⇒aab. There are five production applications, matching 2×3−1. Different expansion orders give the same count because the binary parse structure fixes the number of required nodes.
topics.pitfall: Calling every rule of length at most two CNF. A→B is a unit rule and A→aB mixes a terminal with a nonterminal; both need conversion.

check.question: If A appears twice in B→AA and A is nullable, what shorter alternatives may be needed?
check.answer: B→A and B→ε may be needed, in addition to B→AA. Afterwards remove forbidden epsilon and unit rules while preserving the start-symbol exception.

glossary.meaning: Grammar rules restricted to two variables or one terminal, with a protected start exception.
A variable can derive ε.
A rule A→B containing a single variable on the right.

guided_questions.question: Why introduce a terminal helper?
guided_questions.answer: A binary CNF rule must contain two variables, not a mixture such as aB.

guided_questions.question: How many CNF steps produce four terminals?
guided_questions.answer: Four terminal rules plus three binary rules give 2×4−1=7.

guided_questions.question: Can ε be handled by the same positive-length count?
guided_questions.answer: No. It has no terminal leaves and uses the separate start exception.

instructor_notes.title: Preserve choices before deleting
instructor_notes.body: If a variable can vanish, every relevant occurrence can be kept or omitted. Deleting its ε rule first can silently remove short words.

instructor_notes.title: Normal form is a tool
instructor_notes.body: CNF may add many helper variables. The benefit is a predictable binary parse structure, not necessarily a compact grammar or shorter prose.

worked_problems.title: Convert one length-three rule
worked_problems.question: Grammar S→aBC, B→b, C→c has only the word abc. Convert it to CNF without changing that language.
worked_problems.strategy: First isolate the terminal in the long rule, then split three variables into two-variable steps.
steps: Introduce A→a and replace S→aBC by S→ABC. The generated symbols are unchanged.
Introduce X→BC and replace the long rule with S→AX. Every S step now produces two variables.
Keep B→b and C→c. The rules S→AX, X→BC, A→a, B→b, C→c are all permitted forms.
worked_problems.answer: The CNF grammar still generates exactly abc. It uses two binary and three terminal productions per parse.
worked_problems.sanity_check: For n=3, 2n−1=5 matches those five applications. No alternative rules can generate another word.

worked_problems.title: Remove a repeated nullable variable
worked_problems.question: Grammar S→AA and A→a|ε. Preserve its language using CNF with S allowed as a protected start. S never appears on a right-hand side.
worked_problems.strategy: Enumerate independent keep/drop choices for both A occurrences before removing ε and unit rules.
steps: Keep both A to retain S→AA. Drop one to obtain S→A; dropping either occurrence gives the same rule.
Drop both to retain S→ε. Because S is protected, this empty rule is allowed.
Remove A→ε, leaving A→a. Replace unit S→A by S→a. Final rules are S→AA|a|ε and A→a.
worked_problems.answer: Both grammars generate exactly {ε,a,aa}; the final one is CNF with the stated start exception.
worked_problems.sanity_check: Deleting A→ε without adding S→a and S→ε would lose two of the three words.

topics.title: CYK: build large parses from small spans
topics.story:
A proofreader examines a sentence by first labeling each individual word, then each pair, then each longer segment. A long segment earns a label only when it can be cut into two already understood pieces that match a grammar rule. The table stores useful answers so the proofreader does not rediscover the same segment repeatedly.

CYK follows this plan for CNF grammars. It does not assume that a promising split is the only split; every boundary must be considered. The table answers membership directly, and storing successful choices also allows reconstruction of an actual parse tree.
topics.principle:
Use half-open intervals: T[i,j] is the set of nonterminals deriving the substring w[i:j], with positions 0 through n. Initialize length-one intervals using terminal rules. Then process lengths 2 through n. For every split k strictly between i and j and every rule A→BC, add A when B belongs to T[i,k] and C belongs to T[k,j].

All dependencies have shorter spans, so this order is valid. Accept a nonempty word exactly when the start variable is in T[0,n]. Handle ε separately using the grammar's start exception. With direct scans of binary productions, time is O(|P|n³) and table membership storage is O(|V|n²). For a fixed grammar these become cubic time and quadratic space.
topics.formula:
T[i,i+1] = {A : A→w[i]}
T[i,j] = {A : ∃k, i<k<j, A→BC, B∈T[i,k], C∈T[k,j]}
topics.symbols:
i is an inclusive start position, j an exclusive end position, and k is the boundary between two nonempty substrings. w[i:j] therefore has length j−i. P is the grammar's production set and V its nonterminal set.

T stores sets, not a single winning variable, since one substring may have multiple grammatical roles. The recurrence applies after CNF conversion and only to nonempty spans; empty-input membership is checked separately.
topics.example:
Use S→AB, A→AA | a and B→b. Parse w=aab. Initialize T[0,1]={A}, T[1,2]={A} and T[2,3]={B}. For length two, T[0,2] includes A because A→AA combines the first two cells. T[1,3] includes S because S→AB combines the final a and b.

For T[0,3], split at k=2: A∈T[0,2] and B∈T[2,3], so add S and accept. The shorter cell containing S is not itself enough; acceptance requires S in the cell for the whole string. Recording the successful split reconstructs the tree S(A(A(a),A(a)),B(b)).
topics.pitfall: Mixing inclusive and exclusive endpoints. If T[i,j] denotes w[i:j], its children must be T[i,k] and T[k,j], with no missing or repeated character.

check.question: Why not fill spans in arbitrary order?
check.answer: A cell depends on shorter spans. Increasing length ensures every required subproblem is finished before it is used.

glossary.meaning: A contiguous substring between two boundaries.
Store shorter subproblem answers and reuse them in larger problems.
Include the start position and exclude the end position.

guided_questions.question: Why store a set in each cell?
guided_questions.answer: Several variables may derive the same substring and be useful in different parent rules.

guided_questions.question: What does T[1,3] cover in abc?
guided_questions.answer: Positions 1 and 2, giving bc; position 3 is only the end boundary.

guided_questions.question: Does S in a short cell prove full acceptance?
guided_questions.answer: No. The start variable must appear in the cell spanning the whole word.

instructor_notes.title: Keep all successful splits
instructor_notes.body: Membership needs only whether a variable is present. To recover all parses, retain each successful rule and split rather than just one pointer.

instructor_notes.title: Cubic is a loop structure
instructor_notes.body: There are quadratically many intervals, and each can have linearly many splits. Grammar scanning adds a separate factor; fixed-grammar cubic time does not mean constant cost.

worked_problems.title: Fill a small CYK table
worked_problems.question: CNF grammar S→AC, C→BB, A→a, B→b. Parse abb using boundaries 0,1,2,3.
worked_problems.strategy: Initialize letters and grow spans so every child is available before its parent.
steps: Length-one cells are T[0,1]={A}, T[1,2]={B}, T[2,3]={B}.
For length two, ab has no applicable binary rule, so T[0,2]=∅. The two b cells combine by C→BB, so T[1,3]={C}.
For the full span, split at k=1: A in T[0,1] and C in T[1,3] satisfy S→AC, so add S.
worked_problems.answer: S∈T[0,3], so abb is accepted with tree S(A(a),C(B(b),B(b))).
worked_problems.sanity_check: The grammar has no alternative productions, so its only possible terminal word is indeed abb.

worked_problems.title: Reject despite valid letters
worked_problems.question: Use the same grammar S→AC, C→BB, A→a, B→b and test bab. Explain the whole-span failure.
worked_problems.strategy: Check all possible binary splits, not just whether every letter has a terminal rule.
steps: The diagonal cells for b,a,b are {B},{A},{B}. Every individual letter is known.
Neither ba nor ab matches the only length-two rule C→BB, so both length-two cells are empty.
At k=1 the right span is empty; at k=2 the left span is empty. Neither split can supply A followed by C.
worked_problems.answer: T[0,3]=∅ and bab is rejected. Valid symbols do not guarantee a valid structure.
worked_problems.sanity_check: Compare accepted abb: it alone places an a before the required two-b region.

topics.title: Turing machines and configurations
topics.story:
Picture a meticulous clerk with a long strip of squared paper, a pencil and a small instruction card. The card says what to do based on the clerk's current mode and the symbol in the square under the pencil. One step may replace that symbol, move the pencil one square, and change mode.
