Unlike a finite automaton, the clerk can revisit earlier squares and leave reminders. The strip supplies expandable memory while the instruction card remains finite. Infinite tape is an idealization of unbounded available storage, not a requirement to complete infinitely many operations in one step.
topics.principle:
A Turing machine combines finite control with a read-write tape and a movable head. Its tape alphabet includes the input alphabet plus a blank symbol and possibly markers. A configuration records the current state, head position and tape contents; the transition function determines the next configuration. Most tape cells remain blank after any finite computation.

A machine can halt and accept, halt and reject, or continue forever. When using it as a function computer, specify how the output is encoded on the tape and where the head should finish. Different standard conventions, such as one-sided versus two-sided tape or allowing a stationary move, change descriptions but not which functions are computable. Time and simulation overhead can still differ.
topics.formula:
δ(q,a) = (q′,b,d),  d ∈ {L,R,S}
C₀ ⊢ C₁ ⊢ C₂ ⊢ ⋯
topics.symbols:
q is the current control state, a the symbol under the head, q′ the next state, b the symbol written and d the movement direction. S denotes staying at the same cell.

Cᵢ is the complete configuration after i steps, and ⊢ denotes one valid transition. Halting states have no further computational work. A transition reads the current cell only; the entire tape is not inspected at once.
topics.example:
Design a machine that scans a binary string and replaces every 0 with 1, leaving existing 1s unchanged. In state scan, reading either 0 or 1 writes 1, moves right and stays in scan. Reading blank enters a halting state without changing the tape.

Starting with 010 and the head on its first symbol, the nonblank tape evolves to 110, then 110, then 111. One more transition sees the blank and halts. On empty input it halts immediately. The machine's finite state does not store the whole word; the tape records the evolving output.
topics.pitfall: Treating a missing transition, rejection and infinite looping as interchangeable. State the convention and distinguish halting outcomes from divergence.

check.question: Can a Turing machine have infinitely many states?
check.answer: Not in the standard model. Its control description is finite; unbounded working storage comes from the tape.

glossary.meaning: Current state, head position and tape contents together.
All symbols that may be written, including blank and markers.
One rule that reads, writes, moves and changes state.

guided_questions.question: Why is state alone not a configuration?
guided_questions.answer: The same state can read different cells or symbols and therefore have different next steps.

guided_questions.question: What does a right move from position 2 do?
guided_questions.answer: It makes the next head position 3 after the current cell is written.

guided_questions.question: Does unbounded tape mean infinite work per step?
guided_questions.answer: No. Each step accesses one cell and makes one bounded move.

instructor_notes.title: State output conventions
instructor_notes.body: If a computation leaves useful digits among temporary markers, “the output is on tape” is incomplete. Say which cells form the output and whether markers must be erased.

instructor_notes.title: Count the halting transition
instructor_notes.body: A scanner often needs one extra step to see the first blank after the data. Counting only changed cells can undercount its execution even when some writes do not alter a symbol.

worked_problems.title: Trace a bit-flipping machine
worked_problems.question: In scan, read 0→write 1,R,scan; read 1→write 0,R,scan; read blank→write blank,S,halt. Input 101 occupies positions 0–2, head starts 0. Trace until halt.
worked_problems.strategy: Record both tape and head after each transition; unchanged control state does not mean nothing happened.
steps: At position 0 read 1, write 0 and move to 1. Tape is 001.
At position 1 read 0, write 1 and move to 2. Tape is 011.
At position 2 read 1, write 0 and move to blank position 3. Tape is 010. The fourth transition sees blank and halts there.
worked_problems.answer: Output is 010, with head at 3 after four transitions.
worked_problems.sanity_check: Flipping all output bits again gives original 101, independently checking the transformation.

worked_problems.title: One configuration, one legal next step
worked_problems.question: Tape positions 0,1,2 contain a,b,blank. Head is 1 in q. Rule δ(q,b)=(r,X,L). Compute the next configuration.
worked_problems.strategy: Read the indicated cell, then separate writing, movement and control update.
steps: Head position 1 contains b, so this rule applies; the a at position 0 is not read now.
Replace position 1 by X. The tape becomes a,X,blank while all other cells remain unchanged.
Move left from 1 to 0 and change q to r. The new head reads a only on the next transition.
worked_problems.answer: Next configuration has state r, head 0 and tape aX followed by blanks.
worked_problems.sanity_check: The tape change is local: neither moving left nor changing state erases the a.

topics.title: Designing machines with marking and invariants
topics.story:
A clerk checks pairs of parcels by placing a sticker on one parcel from the left group, walking to the right group and placing a matching sticker there, then returning to repeat. The stickers are memory that survives the clerk's walk.

If the right group runs out too early, or extra unpaired parcels remain at the end, the shipment fails. This pattern is useful when the comparison needs unbounded memory but the machine has only finitely many modes. A good design says what each trip guarantees and why there cannot be infinitely many trips on a finite shipment.
topics.principle:
An implementation-level TM description can use phases rather than enumerate every transition immediately. Define each phase's invariant, the tape markers it expects, and the exit conditions for success or failure. For aⁿbⁿ, first ensure the input has one a block followed by one b block. Repeatedly mark the leftmost unmarked a, find and mark one unmarked b, then return to the left boundary.

Reject if a partner is unavailable; accept only when all a and b symbols are marked. The number of unmarked a symbols strictly decreases on each successful pass, proving termination. Each pass may scan O(n) cells and there are O(n) passes, yielding an O(n²) upper bound for this simple single-tape implementation, not a universal lower bound.
topics.formula:
Invariant after r complete passes: r a-symbols and r b-symbols are marked
Remaining-a count decreases by one per successful pass
topics.symbols:
r counts completed pairing passes. The invariant refers to a tape that has already passed the a*b* shape check, so marked symbols still correspond to two ordered blocks.

The remaining-a count is a nonnegative integer used as a termination measure. n in the running-time bound is total input length. A phase description must also explain boundary detection and malformed inputs before it can be expanded into a fully specified transition table.
topics.example:
Run the pairing method on aaabbb. After the shape check, the first pass produces XaaYbb. The next passes produce XXaYYb and XXXYYY. A final scan sees no unmarked letters and accepts. On aabbb, two passes produce XXYYb; the remaining b causes rejection.

On abab, the shape check rejects before pairing, because a occurs after the b block starts. These three traces test equal counts, unequal counts and incorrect order separately. Merely matching counts would accidentally accept some mixed-order strings outside the target language.
topics.pitfall: Proving that accepted inputs are correct but forgetting termination or failing to reject unmatched symbols. A decider needs both directions and a halting argument.

check.question: Why are marker symbols useful even though states can remember information?
check.answer: Markers preserve an unbounded number of local facts on the tape. A fixed finite state set cannot remember an arbitrary collection of visited positions.

glossary.meaning: A tape symbol recording that a position has been processed.
A group of steps serving one clearly stated purpose.
A nonnegative quantity that strictly decreases during repeated progress.

guided_questions.question: Why check order before pairing?
guided_questions.answer: Equal counts alone would also accept mixed strings such as abab.

guided_questions.question: What does a completed pass guarantee?
guided_questions.answer: Exactly one new a and one new b have been marked.

guided_questions.question: Is the quadratic bound a universal lower bound?
guided_questions.answer: No. It bounds this simple repeated-scan design, not every model or algorithm.

instructor_notes.title: Distinguish failure types
instructor_notes.body: Reject immediately for wrong order, reject when a selected a has no partner, and reject leftover b symbols at the end. Each check closes a different correctness gap.

instructor_notes.title: A decreasing counter needs finite phases
instructor_notes.body: Fewer unmarked a symbols proves finitely many successful passes only if each scan itself reaches a boundary or explicit failure. Include that scan-termination fact.

worked_problems.title: Reject a shortage of partners
worked_problems.question: Use X to mark a and Y to mark b. Run the ordered-block pairing algorithm on aaaabb. Each round marks the leftmost unmarked a and b.
worked_problems.strategy: Trace full successful rounds, then locate the first missing partner.
steps: The shape a*b* is valid. First round pairs one a and b, leaving XaaaYb.
Second round leaves XXaaYY. Two a symbols remain but all b symbols are marked.
Third round selects an a, giving XXXaYY, but the right scan finds no unmarked b before blank. Reject at this explicit failure.
worked_problems.answer: aaaabb is rejected because four a symbols cannot be paired with two b symbols.
worked_problems.sanity_check: Direct counts 4≠2 confirm the outcome; the machine does not need to store the count four in its finite control.

worked_problems.title: Prove the pairing loop halts
worked_problems.question: Input is a finite a-block followed by a b-block, total length n. Each scan ends at a tape boundary or explicit failure. Prove the algorithm cannot complete infinitely many pairing rounds.
worked_problems.strategy: Use unmarked a count as a decreasing nonnegative integer.
steps: Initially let the unmarked a count be u, with 0≤u≤n.
Every successful round marks exactly one previously unmarked a, so the measure changes u→u−1. No rule restores it.
After at most the initial u successful rounds, the count reaches zero. A missing b can reject earlier; the final leftover-b check is a finite scan.
worked_problems.answer: All permitted inputs terminate. Combining at most n rounds with O(n) work per round gives this implementation an O(n²) upper bound.
worked_problems.sanity_check: For u=0 there are no pairing rounds; a final scan still distinguishes ε from a nonempty b-block.

topics.title: Rule tables, description levels and machines with more tapes
topics.story:
Leon is training a new assistant at a small bakery. He explains the same job three ways. To the owner he says: “Every ready cake gets a star.” To the assistant he says: “Walk along the shelf from left to right. Look at the tag on each cake. If it says ready, press a star on the cake and move on. When the shelf ends, stop.” To the safety inspector he hands a rulebook with one line for every situation: “In state WALKING, seeing a READY tag: press a star, step right, stay in WALKING.” The three descriptions are about one job. They differ in how much detail they give.

Then the bakery buys a second shelf, so the assistant can keep the cakes on one shelf and the tags on the other. The assistant is not more skilled, only more comfortable. Anything the assistant does with two shelves, a patient assistant with one shelf can also do, by walking back and forth. That is what “equivalent” means for machines: the same jobs get done, though not always in the same time.
topics.principle:
A Turing machine is a finite rulebook plus a tape. Formally it is a tuple (Q, Σ, Γ, δ, q₀, q_accept, q_reject): the states, the input symbols, the tape symbols (which include the input symbols and a blank), the transition function, the start state and the two halting states. Each rule says: in state q, reading symbol a, write b, move the head one cell or stay, and go to state q′. A transition-rule table lists one row for each pair (state, symbol read). A state diagram draws one circle for each state and one arrow for each rule, labelled a/b,D. The label reads: see a, write b, move D. The table and the diagram hold exactly the same information. Always say what happens when no rule applies. A common convention is that a missing rule means reject.

You can describe a machine at three levels. The high-level description is an algorithm in plain words, with no mention of the tape: “add one to the binary number.” The implementation-level description says what the head does and what is written on the tape, but does not name states: “go to the right end, then move left, turning each 1 into 0, until you reach a 0 or a blank, and write 1.” The formal description gives the tuple and the whole table. Choose the level that the question asks for, and be ready to go down one level. Every sentence at the higher level should match a named group of states and rules.

A multitrack machine has one head and one tape, but each cell holds a stack of symbols, one for each track. With two tracks over the alphabet Γ, a cell holds a pair from Γ × Γ. Rename every pair as a single symbol and you have an ordinary one-tape machine, so tracks add no power. A multitape machine has k tapes and k heads. One rule reads under all k heads, writes under all k heads, moves each head on its own, and changes the one shared state.

Two machines, or two models of machine, are equivalent when they recognize the same languages and compute the same functions. To prove it, simulate in both directions. A one-tape machine is a k-tape machine with k = 1. For the other direction, one tape stores all k tapes side by side, separated by #, with a mark on the symbol under each head. One simulated step takes a sweep to read the marked symbols and another sweep to write them and move the marks. If a tape needs a new cell, everything to its right shifts by one. Equivalent in power does not mean equal in speed: t steps on k tapes can cost about t² steps on one tape.

A small program maps onto these shapes. An assignment such as x = x + 1 becomes a short path of states that changes cells. A sequence of statements becomes a chain: the finishing state of one piece is the starting state of the next. A loop becomes a cycle of states with a test, and the test has one arrow that goes around again and one that exits. A variable becomes a tape, a track, or a region of a tape marked off by #. Say where each head starts and where it ends, because a loop that begins with a head in the wrong place reads the wrong cell.
topics.formula:
M = (Q, Σ, Γ, δ, q₀, q_accept, q_reject)        δ(q, a) = (q′, b, D),   D ∈ {L, R, S}
k tapes:   δ : Q × Γᵏ → Q × Γᵏ × {L, R, S}ᵏ
k tracks:  one head, and each cell holds one symbol of Γᵏ

Binary increment.   Q = {start, carry, halt},   Γ = {0, 1, _}

   state   read   new state   write   move
   start    0      start        0       R
   start    1      start        1       R
   start    _      carry        _       L
   carry    1      carry        0       L
   carry    0      halt         1       S
   carry    _      halt         1       S

   0/0,R 1/1,R              1/0,L
      +---+                  +---+
      |   v                  |   v
 --> (start) --- _/_,L ---> (carry) --- 0/1,S ---> ((halt))
                               |                       ^
                               +-------- _/1,S --------+
topics.symbols:
Q is the finite set of states. Σ is the input alphabet and Γ ⊇ Σ is the tape alphabet. The blank _ belongs to Γ but not to Σ. δ(q, a) = (q′, b, D) gives the next state, the symbol written and the move: L is left, R is right, S is stay. In a label such as 1/0,L, the part before the slash is the symbol read. The part after it is the symbol written, then the move. A double circle, drawn here as (( )), marks a halting state. A machine that computes a function, like the increment machine, can use one halting state in place of q_accept and q_reject.

k is the number of tapes. A track is one layer of a cell. A tape is a separate strip with its own head. # is a separator symbol that does not occur in the input. In the cost estimate later, t counts simulated steps and L is the length of the encoded tape in cells.
topics.example:
Trace the increment machine on 1011, which is eleven in binary. The head starts on the leftmost bit. In state start it moves right over 1, 0, 1, 1 (four steps) and reaches the blank. It steps back onto the last bit in state carry (step 5). That bit is 1, so it writes 0 and moves left (step 6). The next bit is also 1: write 0, move left (step 7). The next bit is 0: write 1 and halt (step 8). The tape reads 1100, which is twelve. For 111 the carry runs off the left end, the rule for a blank writes a new leading 1, and the output is 1000.

Here are the three levels for this machine. High level: “Add one to the binary number.” Implementation level: “Scan right to the first blank, then step back onto the last bit. While the head reads 1, write 0 and move left. When it reads 0 or a blank, write 1 and stop.” Formal level: the table in the formula box.

Now a program with a loop: x = 101 (five), then “repeat 3 times: x = x + 1”. Use two tapes. Tape 1 holds x in binary. Tape 2 holds the counter 111 in unary. State start tests the counter. If the head sees 1, there is another pass to do. If it sees a blank, the machine halts. The states scan, carry and back run the increment on tape 1 and return the head to the left end, and the last rule moves the counter head one cell right, which uses up one 1. The cycle start, scan, carry, back, start is the loop. Scan and carry are the increment, and passing through the states in order is the sequence. At each test, tape 1 holds 101, then 110, then 111, then 1000. The machine halts after 29 steps with x = 1000, which is eight.

To run the same program on one tape, store the two tapes as #101#111# and mark the cell under each head. Each simulated step sweeps across this string two or three times. If the encoded string never exceeds 12 cells, one simulated step costs at most about 3 × 12 = 36 steps on the single tape, so the 29 simulated steps cost about a thousand steps at most. The answer is the same, only slower.
topics.pitfall: Proving equivalence in only one direction, or reading “equivalent” as “equally fast.” A k-tape machine is trivially at least as strong as a one-tape machine, because you can set k = 1. The work is in the other direction, and even then t steps on k tapes can cost about t² steps on one tape.

check.question: Why does a two-track machine need no simulation argument, while a two-tape machine does?
check.answer: A two-track cell holds a pair of symbols under one head. Rename each pair as a single symbol and you already have an ordinary one-tape machine. Two tapes have two heads at different places. One tape must store both strings and remember where each head is, so the simulation needs a real construction.

glossary.meaning: A list of rules, one row for each pair of state and symbol read, giving the new state, the symbol to write and the move.
A drawing with a circle for each state and an arrow for each rule, labelled read/write,move.
One tape and one head, where each cell holds one symbol for every track.
A machine with several tapes, each with its own head, all controlled by one state.
Two models that recognize the same languages and compute the same functions, even if one is slower.

guided_questions.question: What do the three parts of the label 1/0,L mean?
guided_questions.answer: Read 1, write 0, move the head one cell to the left.

guided_questions.question: What changes between the implementation level and the formal level?
guided_questions.answer: The implementation level says what the head does and what is written. The formal level names every state, lists every rule, and states what happens when a rule is missing.

guided_questions.question: How does a loop look in a state diagram?
guided_questions.answer: As a cycle: some state has an arrow back to an earlier one, and a test on the way has a second arrow that leaves the cycle.

guided_questions.question: Why does the single-tape simulation need # between the tapes?
guided_questions.answer: It marks where one tape ends and the next begins. Without it the simulator could not tell which cells belong to which tape.

instructor_notes.title: Pick the level that fits the claim
instructor_notes.body: To prove that a language is decidable, an implementation-level description is usually enough, provided each phase clearly halts and is correct. “Add one” at the high level hides the carry. The implementation level exposes the carry loop, which is where the termination argument lives: each step moves left, so the loop ends at a 0 or at the left end. Use the formal table when the exact detail matters, such as counting steps or giving a tiny machine.

instructor_notes.title: Test a small table on edge inputs
instructor_notes.body: Run the table on the empty input, a single bit, and an input of all 1s. The increment table on the empty input reads a blank in state start, moves to carry, reads a blank again and writes 1, so the output is 1. Decide whether that is acceptable. The table also relies on a blank cell to the left of the number. On a tape that is closed at the left, the carry-out case would need an extra shifting phase, and the table would change.

instructor_notes.title: Equivalence is about power, not speed
instructor_notes.body: Copying a string of n symbols to a second tape takes about n steps on two tapes. On one tape the machine must shuttle back and forth between the two copies, and the cost grows like n². A classical result says that a one-tape machine needs on the order of n² steps to decide whether a string is a palindrome, while a two-tape machine needs only about n. So extra tapes change running time even though they change no language.

worked_problems.title: Turn a table into a diagram and trace it
worked_problems.question: A machine has states even, odd, acc and rej. Its rules are (even,0)→(even,0,R), (even,1)→(odd,1,R), (even,_)→(acc,_,S), (odd,0)→(odd,0,R), (odd,1)→(even,1,R), (odd,_)→(rej,_,S). Draw the diagram as a list of arrows, trace it on 1101, and describe the machine at the high level.
worked_problems.strategy: Turn every row into one labelled arrow. Then follow the head one cell at a time and write the state after each step.
steps: Arrows: even to even labelled 0/0,R; even to odd labelled 1/1,R; even to acc labelled _/_,S; odd to odd labelled 0/0,R; odd to even labelled 1/1,R; odd to rej labelled _/_,S. The start state is even.
Trace on 1101: start in even on the first 1, go to odd; read 1, go to even; read 0, stay in even; read 1, go to odd; read the blank in odd, go to rej.
The machine flips between even and odd at every 1 and ignores 0. Three 1s were seen, so it ends in odd. State odd with a blank rejects.
High-level description: accept exactly the strings that contain an even number of 1s.
worked_problems.answer: The machine rejects 1101, because the string has three 1s. As a high-level description it decides the strings with an even number of 1s.
worked_problems.sanity_check: On the empty input the machine starts in even and reads a blank, so it accepts. Zero is an even number of 1s, so that is correct.

worked_problems.title: Map a small program onto a two-tape machine
worked_problems.question: Program: total = 0; for each 1 on the input: total = total + 1; total = total + 1. Tape 1 holds the input 111 and tape 2 starts blank. The rules (state, tape 1, tape 2) → (state, write 1, write 2, move 1, move 2) are (first,1,_)→(second,1,1,S,R), (second,1,_)→(first,1,1,R,R), (first,_,_)→(halt,_,_,S,S). Trace the machine and identify the increment, the sequence and the loop.
worked_problems.strategy: Follow the state names. Note that the head on tape 2 only ever moves right, so tape 2 behaves like a counter that grows.
steps: Step 1: state first reads 1 on tape 1 and a blank on tape 2. It writes 1 on tape 2, moves that head right and goes to second. Tape 2 holds 1.
Step 2: state second reads 1 and a blank. It writes another 1 on tape 2, moves both heads right and goes to first. Tape 2 holds 11 and the input head has moved on by one cell.
Steps 3 to 6 repeat the same pair for the second and third 1. Tape 2 holds 1111 after step 4 and 111111 after step 6.
Step 7: state first reads a blank on tape 1 and halts. The machine used 2 × 3 + 1 = 7 steps.

The increment is the write-1-and-move-right on tape 2, which occurs once in first and once in second. The sequence is first then second. The loop is the arrow from second back to first, with the test on tape 1 deciding between going around and halting.
worked_problems.answer: The output is 111111, which is six 1s for the three input symbols: the loop added 2 to the total on each pass.
worked_problems.sanity_check: With the empty input the machine halts at once with tape 2 empty, matching zero passes of the loop.

worked_problems.title: Count tracks and price a simulation
worked_problems.question: Part (a): a machine with 3 tracks uses the symbols 0, 1 and blank on every track. How many different symbols does the equivalent one-track machine need? Part (b): a 2-tape machine halts after 29 steps. Its encoding on one tape never exceeds 12 cells, and each simulated step costs at most 3 sweeps. Give an upper bound on the one-tape steps.
worked_problems.strategy: For (a), count the possible columns of a cell. For (b), multiply the steps by the cost of one simulated step.
steps: A cell is a column with 3 entries, and each entry is one of 3 symbols. There are 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 possible columns.
The one-track machine uses each column as one symbol, so its tape alphabet has 27 symbols, including the all-blank column.
One sweep costs at most 12 steps, so one simulated step costs at most 3 × 12 = 36 steps.
For 29 simulated steps the total is at most 29 × 36 = 1044 steps.
worked_problems.answer: The one-track machine needs 27 symbols, and the one-tape simulation takes at most 1044 steps. The language or function is unchanged.
worked_problems.sanity_check: The count 27 is 3 raised to the power 3, so with k tracks and a symbols per track the alphabet has aᵏ symbols. With one track it gives a, as it should.

code_examples.title: Run a rule table on one tape and on two
code_examples.intro: Mia keeps her machine rules as data. A rule table is a Python dictionary from (state, symbols read) to (new state, symbols written, moves). One small simulator runs any table with any number of tapes. The first table adds one to a binary number on one tape. The second runs the program “repeat 3 times: x = x + 1” on two tapes.
code_examples.code:
def run_tm(rules, tapes, start="start", halt="halt", limit=500):
    """Run a deterministic k-tape machine. Every tape starts with its head on cell 0.

    rules maps (state, symbols read) to (new state, symbols written, moves)."""
    cells = [dict(enumerate(t)) for t in tapes]
    heads = [0] * len(tapes)
    state, steps, history = start, 0, []

    def snapshot():
        shown = []
        for tape, head in zip(cells, heads):
            used = [i for i, c in tape.items() if c != "_"] + [head]
            lo, hi = min(used), max(used)
            shown.append("".join(f"[{tape.get(i, '_')}]" if i == head else tape.get(i, "_")
                                 for i in range(lo, hi + 1)))
        return state, shown

    history.append(snapshot())
    while state != halt:
        read = tuple(t.get(h, "_") for t, h in zip(cells, heads))
        if (state, read) not in rules:
            raise RuntimeError(f"no rule for {state} reading {read}")
        state, write, moves = rules[(state, read)]
        for i, (w, m) in enumerate(zip(write, moves)):
            cells[i][heads[i]] = w
            heads[i] += {"L": -1, "R": 1, "S": 0}[m]
        steps += 1
        history.append(snapshot())
        if steps > limit:
            raise RuntimeError("step limit reached")
    return steps, history


def contents(history):
    return [t.replace("[", "").replace("]", "").strip("_") for t in history[-1][1]]


# One tape: add 1 to a binary number. Rules: (state, (read,)) -> (state, (write,), (move,))
increment = {}
for bit in "01":
    increment[("start", (bit,))] = ("start", (bit,), "R")      # walk to the right end
increment[("start", ("_",))] = ("carry", ("_",), "L")           # step back onto the last bit
increment[("carry", ("1",))] = ("carry", ("0",), "L")           # 1 plus carry: write 0, carry on
increment[("carry", ("0",))] = ("halt", ("1",), "S")            # 0 plus carry: write 1, done
increment[("carry", ("_",))] = ("halt", ("1",), "S")            # ran off the left end: new leading 1

for text in ("1011", "111"):
    steps, history = run_tm(increment, [text])
    print(f"one tape : {text} + 1 = {contents(history)[0]} in {steps} steps")

# Two tapes: tape 1 holds x in binary, tape 2 holds a unary counter.
# Program:  repeat 3 times: x = x + 1
loop = {}
for bit in "01":
    loop[("start", (bit, "1"))] = ("scan", (bit, "1"), "SS")    # counter left? do one more pass
    loop[("start", (bit, "_"))] = ("halt", (bit, "_"), "SS")    # counter empty: finished
    loop[("scan", (bit, "1"))] = ("scan", (bit, "1"), "RS")     # find the end of x
    loop[("back", (bit, "1"))] = ("back", (bit, "1"), "LS")     # return to the start of x
loop[("scan", ("_", "1"))] = ("carry", ("_", "1"), "LS")
loop[("carry", ("1", "1"))] = ("carry", ("0", "1"), "LS")       # the increment, as before
loop[("carry", ("0", "1"))] = ("back", ("1", "1"), "LS")
loop[("carry", ("_", "1"))] = ("back", ("1", "1"), "LS")
loop[("back", ("_", "1"))] = ("start", ("_", "1"), "RR")        # count one pass, loop again

steps, history = run_tm(loop, ["101", "111"])
print(f"two tapes: x = 101, counter 111 -> x = {contents(history)[0]} in {steps} steps")
for state, (tape1, tape2) in history:
    if state == "start":
        print(f"  at the loop test: x = {tape1:<8} counter = {tape2}")
code_examples.output:
one tape : 1011 + 1 = 1100 in 8 steps
one tape : 111 + 1 = 1000 in 8 steps
two tapes: x = 101, counter 111 -> x = 1000 in 29 steps
  at the loop test: x = [1]01    counter = [1]11
  at the loop test: x = [1]10    counter = 1[1]1
  at the loop test: x = [1]11    counter = 11[1]
  at the loop test: x = [1]000   counter = 111[_]
walkthrough: run_tm keeps one dictionary of cells and one head position for each tape. A cell that is not in the dictionary is blank.

Each step reads one symbol from every tape, looks up the rule, writes under every head, moves every head and changes the state. A missing rule raises an error, which is this program’s convention for a crash.
The increment table has six rules: two for walking right over bits, one for turning back at the blank, and three for the carry. The start state is start and the halting state is halt.

The loop table adds a second tape. A 1 under the counter head means one more pass is due. State start tests it, the states scan, carry and back run the increment and return to the left end, and the last rule moves the counter head one cell right.
snapshot builds the strings that are printed and traced: the cell under each head is written in brackets.
code_examples.explanation:
The first two output lines show that the increment machine takes 8 steps on both 1011 and 111, although the second input carries all the way. For 1011, walking right takes 5 steps (four bits, then the blank) and the carry takes 3. For 111 the walk takes 4 steps and the carry takes 4, because the final carry lands on a blank and writes a new leading 1.

The loop machine prints the value of x each time it re-enters state start, which is each test of the counter. The values are 101, 110, 111 and 1000. The brackets show where the heads are. After the third pass the counter head sits on a blank, so the next test ends the loop. The machine halts after 29 steps.

Look for the three shapes. The increment is the pair of states scan and carry. The sequence is passing through scan, carry and back in order. The loop is the rule that returns from back to start. Because the counter has its own tape, it never disturbs the number. On a single tape, you would need a region marked off for the counter and a trip to it on every pass.

topics.title: Simulation, universality and the Church–Turing thesis
topics.story:
A universal music player can perform many pieces because it reads a score supplied as data. Its hardware does not need to be rebuilt for every melody. A universal Turing machine similarly reads an encoded machine description together with that machine's input. It interprets the description step by step.

The analogy also exposes a limitation: following a score does not reveal in advance whether a strange score instructs the player to repeat forever. Universality is the power to simulate arbitrary encoded programs, not the power to predict every program's eventual behavior without executing it.
topics.principle:
A universal TM U simulates a machine M on input w from a finite encoding ⟨M,w⟩. It preserves the simulated outcome: acceptance, rejection or nontermination. Machine descriptions can be data because finite alphabets, states and transition tables admit finite string encodings. Equivalence between two formal computation models is established by simulations in both directions; one simulation alone proves only containment of power.

The Church–Turing thesis identifies effective algorithmic computation with Turing computability. It is a thesis about the informal notion of an algorithm, not a theorem proved merely by defining a TM. Specific simulation theorems, including universality and equivalence of standard tape variants, are mathematical results. Computational equivalence says nothing by itself about equal speed, memory cost or practical usability.
topics.formula:
U(⟨M,w⟩) simulates M(w)
M(w) accepts/rejects/diverges ⇒ U(⟨M,w⟩) has the same outcome
topics.symbols:
⟨M,w⟩ is a computable encoding of a finite machine description and a finite input string, with enough structure to separate them. U is one fixed machine, while M ranges over encoded machines. “Diverges” means the computation never halts.

The displayed relationship concerns behavior, not the number of simulation steps. A valid encoding also needs a defined treatment of malformed descriptions, commonly immediate rejection.
topics.example:
Suppose M is a machine that writes one additional 1 after a unary input and then halts. Give U the encoding of M together with 111. U stores a simulated state and head position, looks up the applicable encoded rule, updates a representation of the simulated tape, and repeats until M's halting state appears.

The simulated output is 1111. Now give U a different machine whose only behavior is moving right forever. U also continues forever. Both cases are handled by the same interpreter, demonstrating universality while showing why it does not provide a halting test.
topics.pitfall: Saying that the Church–Turing thesis proves all imaginable physical devices equivalent to TMs, or that simulation guarantees equal efficiency.

check.question: Does a Python simulator of TMs alone prove that Python and TMs have equal power?
check.answer: No. It shows Python can simulate TMs. The reverse direction, simulating the relevant Python computation model with TMs, is also required.

glossary.meaning: A finite string representing a machine or input.
One interpreter able to simulate encoded machines.
Extra work needed to reproduce another model’s steps.

guided_questions.question: Why can a machine description be input data?
guided_questions.answer: Its finite rules can be listed and encoded using finite symbols.

guided_questions.question: Does simulating a loop make it halt?
guided_questions.answer: No. A faithful simulation preserves nontermination.

guided_questions.question: Why need both simulation directions?
guided_questions.answer: One direction proves only that the simulator is at least as expressive as the simulated model.

instructor_notes.title: Behavior and resources are separate
instructor_notes.body: Two models can compute the same functions while taking very different numbers of steps. State both the preserved result and the resource relationship when discussing a simulation.

instructor_notes.title: Malformed encodings are ordinary inputs too
instructor_notes.body: A universal interpreter must recognize where the machine description ends and reject invalid formats according to a stated convention. Otherwise its formal input behavior is incomplete.

worked_problems.title: Simulate a simple incrementer
worked_problems.question: Machine M scans right across unary 1s, writes one additional 1 at the first blank, and halts. Input is 11, head on its first symbol. Describe the simulated output and steps.
worked_problems.strategy: Keep simulated tape, head and state; apply one encoded rule at a time.
steps: First scan step reads position 0=1, leaves it unchanged, and moves to position 1.
Second scan step reads position 1=1 and moves to blank position 2.
The next rule writes 1 at position 2 and enters halt. The simulated tape now contains 111.
worked_problems.answer: The simulated output is 111, representing unary three. M uses three transitions under this stated convention.
worked_problems.sanity_check: The universal interpreter may use more than three of its own transitions to implement those three simulated steps.

worked_problems.title: Track explicit simulation overhead
worked_problems.question: A toy interpreter needs 6 of its own steps per simulated step and 10 setup steps. The simulated program halts after 7 steps. Find total interpreter work; then discuss a nonhalting simulated program.
worked_problems.strategy: Separate fixed setup from repeated per-step cost, then distinguish finite cost from preserved divergence.
steps: Seven simulated steps cost 7×6=42 interpreter steps.
Add setup once: 42+10=52. This is a cost model supplied by the question, not a universal bound.
If the simulated program takes infinitely many steps, reproducing every step requires infinitely many interpreter steps too.
worked_problems.answer: The halting example costs 52 steps. Faithful simulation of the nonhalting example also never halts.
worked_problems.sanity_check: At zero simulated steps only setup remains, giving 10, consistent with the formula 10+6t.

topics.title: Recognizers versus deciders
topics.story:
A lost-property office can confirm that your bag has arrived when someone finds a matching tag. If it has not arrived, the clerk might keep searching indefinitely. A different office promises to finish checking a complete finite register and answer either yes or no.

The first behavior resembles recognition; the second resembles decision. Waiting a very long time at the first office does not turn silence into a reliable no. The difference is a guarantee about all inputs, not a difference in how friendly or fast the clerk seems on the requests observed so far.
topics.principle:
A recognizer for a language must accept every member and must never accept a nonmember. On nonmembers it may reject or run forever. A decider additionally halts on every input, so every membership question receives a correct yes or no.

Every decidable language is recognizable, but not every recognizable language is decidable. For encoded machine acceptance, universal simulation recognizes yes instances: if the simulated machine accepts, eventually that event is observed. If it rejects, the recognizer can reject; if it loops, the recognizer may loop.

Finite testing cannot establish that a program is a decider, because an untested input could diverge. A proof requires an argument that all permitted computations terminate as well as an argument that their answers are correct.
topics.symbols:
L(M) records only accepted strings; rejected and divergent computations are both outside this language. Σ* is the universe of finite input strings under the chosen encoding.

The strict inclusion symbol means every decidable language is recognizable and at least one recognizable language is not decidable. This classification describes existence of some appropriate machine, not whether a particular poorly designed implementation happens to terminate.
topics.example:
Consider a program that examines candidates 0,1,2,… and accepts if it finds an integer x satisfying an input predicate P(x). Suppose each individual predicate check halts. If a witness exists, the program eventually reaches one and accepts. If none exists, the search continues forever.

Thus it recognizes the witness-existence property but does not automatically decide it. For P(x) meaning x²=49 it accepts at x=7. For P(x) meaning x²=50 over nonnegative integers it keeps searching, even though a human can design a better bounded procedure for this special predicate family. One looping implementation does not prove a language undecidable.
topics.pitfall: Inferring nonmembership from a timeout, or inferring undecidability merely because one attempted algorithm loops.

check.question: Can a recognizable language have a recognizer that rejects some nonmembers and loops on others?
check.answer: Yes. Both behaviors are permitted outside the language. The only forbidden behavior there is acceptance.

glossary.meaning: Accepts every member and never accepts a nonmember; it may loop on nonmembers.
Gives a correct membership answer and halts on every input.
A finite object that establishes a yes answer.

guided_questions.question: What can silence from a recognizer mean?
guided_questions.answer: It may not have found a future witness yet, or it may search forever; silence alone distinguishes neither.

guided_questions.question: Why is every decider also a recognizer?
guided_questions.answer: Its correct accepting behavior satisfies recognition, with the stronger guarantee of stopping on no instances too.

guided_questions.question: Can a poor recognizer exist for a decidable language?
guided_questions.answer: Yes. Decidability concerns existence of some decider, not quality of every implementation.

instructor_notes.title: A proof needs universal termination
instructor_notes.body: Showing ten traces stop proves only those ten cases. A bound or decreasing measure covering every allowed input supplies the missing general argument.

instructor_notes.title: Restrictions may make search finite
instructor_notes.body: An unbounded witness search becomes a decider if a computable finite bound is proven sufficient. The bound must come from the problem, not an arbitrary timeout.

worked_problems.title: A recognizer that loops on a simple no case
worked_problems.question: For input n≥0, test x=0,1,2,… and accept when x²=n. Each square test halts. Compare inputs 16 and 18.
worked_problems.strategy: Separate existence of a witness from termination when no witness exists.
steps: For n=16, squares tested are 0,1,4,9,16, so x=4 supplies a witness and the program accepts.
For n=18, 4²=16 and 5²=25. Later nonnegative squares only grow, so no x satisfies the equation.
The specified program has no rule to stop after passing n. It keeps trying forever on 18 despite the available mathematical rejection argument.
worked_problems.answer: This program recognizes perfect squares but does not decide them. It accepts 16 and diverges on 18.
worked_problems.sanity_check: A different program can reject as soon as x²>n. Thus the looping example does not prove the square language undecidable.

worked_problems.title: Turn the special search into a decider
worked_problems.question: Modify square search: for integer n≥0, test x from 0 through n inclusive; accept on equality x²=n and otherwise reject after the loop. Prove correctness and termination.
worked_problems.strategy: Show the finite range contains every possible nonnegative square root.
steps: For n=0, only x=0 is needed and it succeeds. For n≥1, any x>n has x²≥x>n, so cannot be a solution.
The loop checks n+1 candidates and each test halts, so total execution is finite.
An equality gives a genuine square witness. If none occurs in the sufficient range, no nonnegative integer solution exists, so rejection is correct.
worked_problems.answer: The bounded procedure decides perfect-square membership. A tighter bound could improve speed without changing the answer.
worked_problems.sanity_check: For n=1, x=1 is included. Omitting the upper endpoint would incorrectly reject this boundary case.

topics.title: Why universal termination tests cannot exist
topics.story:
Imagine a catalogue that claims to classify every possible catalogue-checking program, including programs that read their own catalogue entry. A mischievous program can inspect the prediction about itself and deliberately do the opposite. This self-reference creates a contradiction if the catalogue is always correct and always answers.

The argument does not depend on a machine being too slow or lacking enough memory. It attacks the possibility of a complete procedure. Real analysis tools remain useful because they can restrict the programs considered, permit uncertainty, or settle for guarantees that do not answer every question about every program.
topics.principle:
Assume a total algorithm H decides whether any encoded machine halts on any input. Construct a machine D that, on a machine description x, asks H whether x halts on input x. If H says yes, D loops forever; if H says no, D halts. Evaluate D on its own description.

Either answer from H contradicts D's defined behavior, so no such total correct H exists. The halting language is nevertheless recognizable by simulation until any halting outcome occurs. Acceptance is also recognizable but undecidable.

A related diagonal language, consisting of machine descriptions whose machines do not accept their own descriptions, is not recognizable: any proposed recognizer disagrees with it on its own description. Encodings and malformed inputs must be handled consistently in formal proofs.
topics.formula:
HALT = {⟨M,w⟩ : M halts on w}
D(x): if H(x,x)=yes then loop; otherwise halt
topics.symbols:
H is a hypothetical decider, so its answer is assumed to arrive on every well-formed pair. x encodes a machine and is also a legal input string to that machine.

D is a finite program using H as a subroutine. Substituting x=⟨D⟩ forces the contradiction. HALT includes both accepting and rejecting halts; it is different from the language of accepting computations alone.
topics.example:
Suppose the hypothetical H predicts that D halts on ⟨D⟩. By its rule, D sees yes and deliberately loops, making the prediction false. Suppose instead H predicts that D does not halt. D sees no and immediately halts, again making the prediction false. These two cases exhaust the Boolean answers of a decider.

Adding a third “unknown” outcome avoids the contradiction but fails to decide the original problem. Restricting attention to programs with a fixed step limit also avoids it, because those programs can simply be simulated up to the limit; that is a different input class.
topics.pitfall: Concluding that no program can ever prove another program terminates. The theorem excludes one complete, always-correct decider for all programs and inputs.

check.question: Why does this proof require H to halt on every input?
check.answer: D must receive H’s answer before choosing its opposite behavior. If H can loop or say unknown, the contradiction no longer establishes a complete decision procedure.

glossary.meaning: No algorithm always halts with the correct answer for every allowed input.
Use a construction’s own description to force disagreement.
An algorithm guaranteed to halt on every input in its domain.

guided_questions.question: What is assumed about H?
guided_questions.answer: It answers every well-formed machine-input pair correctly and always halts.

guided_questions.question: What does D do after a yes prediction?
guided_questions.answer: It deliberately loops, contradicting a prediction that it halts.

guided_questions.question: Does unknown escape the contradiction?
guided_questions.answer: It can, but then H is not a decider for every input.

instructor_notes.title: Do not confuse halting with accepting
instructor_notes.body: A program that halts and rejects belongs to HALT. A recognizer for HALT therefore accepts after either simulated halt, not only after simulated acceptance.

instructor_notes.title: Useful tools remain possible
instructor_notes.body: A checker can prove termination for a restricted loop language with a decreasing integer counter. This does not conflict with the theorem, whose domain includes arbitrary programs.

worked_problems.title: Complete the self-reference cases
worked_problems.question: Assume H is a total correct halting decider. Define D(x) to loop if H(x,x)=yes and halt if H(x,x)=no. Evaluate H on (⟨D⟩,⟨D⟩).
worked_problems.strategy: Exhaust the two possible Boolean answers rather than guessing which occurs.
steps: If H returns yes, it predicts D halts on its own description. But D’s yes branch loops forever.
If H returns no, it predicts D does not halt there. But D’s no branch halts immediately.
Because H is total, it must return one of these answers. Both contradict correctness, so the starting assumption fails.
worked_problems.answer: No total correct halting decider H exists for arbitrary encoded programs and inputs.
worked_problems.sanity_check: If H may fail to return, step three is unavailable. The proof targets complete deciders, not partial tools.

worked_problems.title: A bounded question is decidable
worked_problems.question: Given a finite machine description M, input w and nonnegative integer B, decide whether M halts within at most B transitions. Explain a correct procedure, including B=0.
worked_problems.strategy: The supplied finite bound permits complete simulation up to that bound; answer only the bounded question.
steps: Inspect the initial configuration. If it is already a designated halting configuration, answer yes even when B=0.
Otherwise perform at most B legal transitions, checking after each whether a halting state was reached. Answer yes if it was.
If none of those checked configurations halts, answer no to “within B”. The counter bounds the simulation, so this procedure itself terminates.
worked_problems.answer: Bounded halting is decidable. A no answer means no halt within the bound, not never halting.
worked_problems.sanity_check: A machine halting at B+1 is correctly rejected by this bounded question but belongs to unrestricted HALT.

topics.title: Dovetailing and complement
topics.story:
Two investigators search for opposite certificates about the same claim. One looks for evidence that the claim is true; the other looks for evidence that it is false. If you let the first investigator monopolize the room until finishing, the second may never get a turn. Instead, give them alternating time slots.

When one is guaranteed eventually to find the appropriate certificate, alternating effort guarantees a conclusion. This scheduling idea is dovetailing. It does not magically make an impossible certificate appear: its force comes from knowing that every case belongs to exactly one of the two searchable sides.
topics.principle:
Decidable languages are closed under complement, union and intersection because their deciders always finish. Swapping acceptance and rejection complements a decider. Recognizable languages are closed under union and intersection, but complement is not guaranteed. For union, simulate both recognizers fairly and accept when either accepts; sequentially waiting for the first can get stuck even if the second would accept.

For intersection, accept after both have accepted, using fair simulation as a uniform construction. A language is decidable exactly when both it and its complement are recognizable. To prove the reverse direction, dovetail the two recognizers; one must eventually accept, determining the answer. This theorem explains why the complement of a recognizable undecidable language cannot also be recognizable.
topics.formula:
L is decidable ⇔ L and Σ*∖L are recognizable
Union recognizer: accept when R₁ or R₂ accepts
Intersection recognizer: accept after both accept
topics.symbols:
Σ* fixes the entire universe of input strings, so complement includes every string outside L. R₁ and R₂ are recognizers, each with its own simulated configuration.

Fair simulation gives each unfinished process unboundedly many steps, for example alternating one step each. Acceptance flags can be remembered after a process halts. On a nonmember a combined recognizer may still run forever, which is consistent with recognition.
topics.example:
Let Ryes recognize a language L and Rno recognize its complement. On an input z, suppose Ryes would loop forever while Rno accepts after 37 steps. A sequential strategy that waits for Ryes first never answers. Alternating one step of each simulator reaches the accepting event of Rno after at most 74 simulated steps, so the combined procedure rejects z.

If instead z belongs to L, Ryes is the process guaranteed eventually to accept. The combined procedure halts in either case. The guarantee requires complementary languages; two unrelated searches might both run forever on the same input.
topics.pitfall: Complementing a recognizer by swapping halting labels. Its infinite computations remain infinite, so previously unaccepted inputs do not all become accepted.

check.question: If L is recognizable and undecidable, what can be said about its complement?
check.answer: Its complement is not recognizable. Otherwise recognizers for both sides could be dovetailed to decide L, contradicting undecidability.

glossary.meaning: Share steps fairly among simulations so none waits forever for another.
All allowed input strings outside the language.
A remembered fact that a simulation has already accepted.

guided_questions.question: Why not run one recognizer to completion first?
guided_questions.answer: It may never finish on this input, preventing the other from finding a witness.

guided_questions.question: What must an intersection recognizer remember?
guided_questions.answer: Whether each component has accepted; accept only after both flags are true.

guided_questions.question: Why do complementary recognizers give a decider?
guided_questions.answer: Every input belongs to exactly one side, whose recognizer is guaranteed eventually to accept.

instructor_notes.title: Fairness is an algorithmic promise
instructor_notes.body: Alternating one step per live process is sufficient. Merely saying “try both” is incomplete if an implementation can give one process no further turns.

instructor_notes.title: Rejection is not a certificate of complement recognition
instructor_notes.body: A recognizer may reject some outsiders but loop on others. Reusing only its rejections cannot cover every member of the complement.

worked_problems.title: Count fair simulation steps
worked_problems.question: Ryes recognizes L and Rno its complement. On input w, Ryes loops and Rno accepts on its fifth own step. Alternate Ryes then Rno, one step each. Find when the combined decider answers.
worked_problems.strategy: Number global simulated steps and track which machine receives each one.
steps: Global steps 1,3,5,7,9 go to Ryes; they do not terminate its search.
Global steps 2,4,6,8,10 are Rno’s first through fifth steps. At global step 10 it accepts.
Acceptance by the complement recognizer certifies w∉L, so the combined machine rejects immediately.
worked_problems.answer: The decider rejects after 10 simulated component steps, excluding scheduler bookkeeping.
worked_problems.sanity_check: Sequentially waiting for Ryes would never reach any Rno step, despite the five-step certificate.

worked_problems.title: Why the complement cannot also be recognizable
worked_problems.question: Assume L is recognizable and undecidable. Suppose, for contradiction, that its complement has a recognizer C. Derive the contradiction without assuming either recognizer halts on all inputs.
worked_problems.strategy: Combine two partial successes with fair scheduling and membership exclusivity.
steps: Run the given recognizer R for L and C for its complement in alternating steps on the same input.
If the input belongs to L, R eventually accepts; otherwise C eventually accepts. Neither can accept on the wrong side.
Accept when R accepts and reject when C accepts. Every input therefore receives a correct terminating answer.
worked_problems.answer: This constructs a decider for L, contradicting the premise. Hence its complement is not recognizable.
worked_problems.sanity_check: For a decidable language there is no contradiction: both it and its complement have deciders and hence recognizers.

topics.title: Proving new languages undecidable or unrecognizable
topics.story:
Noah announces that he has built a checker. Hand it the manual of any machine, he says, and it tells you at once whether that machine accepts at least one input. Iris doubts him. She does not test the checker on thousands of manuals. She asks a different question: if this checker really worked, what else could I do with it?

Iris already knows one job that nobody can do. Given a machine M and an input w, decide whether M accepts w. She sees a trick. From M and w she writes a new manual M_w. The new machine ignores every input except w, and on w it follows M. So M_w accepts something exactly when M accepts w. Iris hands M_w to Noah's checker and reads the answer. If the checker worked, Iris would have solved the job that nobody can solve. So it cannot work.

Notice that Iris only writes the new manual. She never follows it. Writing takes a few minutes. Following it could take forever.
topics.principle:
To show that a new language L is undecidable, pick a language A that is already known to be undecidable. The usual choice is A_TM, the pairs ⟨M,w⟩ where machine M accepts input w. Assume, for contradiction, that a decider R for L exists. Use R as a subroutine to build a machine S that decides A. No such S can exist, so R cannot exist either.

A complete proof has five parts: the assumption, the construction of S, a proof that S is right when the answer is yes, a proof that S is right when the answer is no, and a proof that S halts on every input. The last part is the one people forget. It usually rests on two facts: the construction step only writes a finite string, and R is a decider, so it always answers.

The same idea has a compact form. A mapping reduction from A to B is a computable function f, defined on every string, such that w is in A exactly when f(w) is in B. We write A ≤m B. If B is decidable, so is A: compute f(w), then ask B's decider. If B is recognizable, so is A. Read the other way round, these are the tools we use. If A is not decidable, B is not decidable. If A is not recognizable, B is not recognizable. The direction matters: the language you already know is hard goes on the left, and the new language goes on the right.

Closure properties give a second route that is often shorter. Decidable languages are closed under complement, union, intersection and difference, because deciders always halt and their answers can be combined. Recognizable languages are closed under union and intersection, but not under complement. One fact links the two classes: a language is decidable exactly when both it and its complement are recognizable. So to show L is not decidable, assume it is, and combine it with a decidable language, using a closure rule, to rebuild a known undecidable language. To show L is not recognizable, show that its complement is recognizable but undecidable.
topics.formula:
A ≤m B  :  a computable f, defined on every string, with  w ∈ A  ⇔  f(w) ∈ B

A ≤m B and B decidable           ⇒  A decidable
A ≤m B and B recognizable        ⇒  A recognizable
A ≤m B and A not decidable       ⇒  B not decidable
A ≤m B and A not recognizable    ⇒  B not recognizable

L decidable  ⇔  L and its complement are both recognizable

Proof that L is undecidable:
  1. Suppose R decides L.
  2. S on input ⟨M,w⟩: write ⟨M′⟩ ; run R on ⟨M′⟩ ; answer (possibly flipped).
  3. Show  M accepts w  ⇔  S accepts   (both directions).
  4. Show S halts on every input.
  5. So S decides A_TM. Contradiction.
topics.symbols:
A_TM = {⟨M,w⟩ : M accepts w} and HALT_TM = {⟨M,w⟩ : M halts on w} are the two standard undecidable languages. A_TM is recognizable, because we can simulate M on w, but its complement is not recognizable. The notation ⟨M⟩ is a string that describes machine M, so that other machines can take it as input. L(M) is the set of strings that M accepts. E_TM = {⟨M⟩ : L(M) = ∅} is the language of machines that accept nothing. By convention, a string that is not a valid code counts as the code of a machine that accepts nothing.

M′ and M_w are machines that S writes down. They depend on M and w. The function f in a mapping reduction plays the role of step 2: it is a program that always finishes and outputs a description. Σ* is the set of all strings, and the complement of L is Σ* ∖ L.
topics.example:
Claim: E_TM is not decidable. Proof. Suppose R decides E_TM. Build S. On input ⟨M,w⟩, S writes the code of the machine M_w, defined as follows. On input x, M_w rejects if x is not w. If x is w, it runs M on w, and it accepts if M accepts. Then S runs R on ⟨M_w⟩. If R accepts, S rejects. If R rejects, S accepts.

Check both directions. If M accepts w, then M_w accepts w and nothing else. So L(M_w) = {w} is not empty, R rejects ⟨M_w⟩, and S accepts. If M does not accept w, because it rejects or loops, then M_w never accepts anything. So L(M_w) = ∅, R accepts, and S rejects. S always halts: writing ⟨M_w⟩ means copying ⟨M⟩ and w into a fixed template, and R always answers. So S decides A_TM, which is impossible. Therefore R does not exist.

Take a concrete M that accepts a string exactly when it has an even number of 1s. For w = 1001 there are two 1s, so M accepts, L(M_w) = {1001} and S answers yes. For w = 1011 there are three 1s, so M rejects, L(M_w) = ∅ and S answers no. If M loops on w, then M_w loops on w, L(M_w) is still empty, and S still answers no.

Now the unrecognizable half. The complement of E_TM is the set of codes of machines that accept at least one string. That language is recognizable: run M on the strings 0, 1, 00, 01, … in a fair interleaving, and accept as soon as one run accepts. If E_TM were also recognizable, then E_TM would be decidable, which we just ruled out. So E_TM is not recognizable.
topics.pitfall: Reducing in the wrong direction. If you show that the known-hard language can be solved using the new one, you prove something. If you show that the new language can be solved using the known-hard one, you prove only that the new language is no harder, which says nothing about whether it is decidable.

check.question: In the proof that E_TM is undecidable, why can S safely build M_w even when M loops forever on w?
check.answer: Building M_w means writing a description: copy the code of M and the string w into a fixed template. M is never run during that step, so the step always finishes. M_w would loop on w, but S never runs M_w either. It gives the description to R, and R, being a decider, always answers.

glossary.meaning: A computable rewrite that turns a question about one language into a question about another.
A decider that we assume exists only so that we can derive a contradiction from it.
A string that describes machine M, so that another machine can take it as input.
A class of languages is closed under an operation if applying the operation to members always gives a member.
The fixed piece of machine behavior that the construction wraps around M and w.

guided_questions.question: Which language do we assume has a decider?
guided_questions.answer: The new language L, the one we want to prove undecidable. We never assume anything about the known-hard language except that it is undecidable.

guided_questions.question: What does the machine S decide at the end of the proof?
guided_questions.answer: A known undecidable language such as A_TM. That is why the contradiction appears.

guided_questions.question: Why must we prove both directions of “M accepts w exactly when S accepts”?
guided_questions.answer: With only one direction, S could still be wrong on some inputs, for example rejecting a pair that M really accepts. Then S would not decide A_TM.

guided_questions.question: How does closure under complement help?
guided_questions.answer: If L were decidable, swapping the yes and no answers would decide the complement. So the complement of an undecidable language is undecidable too.

instructor_notes.title: Choose the gadget by asking what the target language tests
instructor_notes.body: E_TM tests whether any string is accepted, so M_w is built to accept something exactly when M accepts w. For the language of machines whose language is regular, M_w must have a regular language exactly when M accepts w. Let M_w accept every string of the form 0ⁿ1ⁿ, and on every other string run M on w and accept if M accepts. If M accepts w, L(M_w) is Σ*, which is regular. If not, L(M_w) is {0ⁿ1ⁿ}, which is not regular. The recipe stays the same. Only the gadget changes.

instructor_notes.title: A property of the code itself is easy to decide
instructor_notes.body: The question “does M have more than five states?” can be answered by reading ⟨M⟩, so it is decidable, and no gadget can tie it to acceptance. A reduction proof works only when the property depends on what the machine does, not on how it is written. Use this as a quick check before you start a proof.

instructor_notes.title: Closure arguments need a decidable partner
instructor_notes.body: If X is decidable and D is decidable, then X ∩ D, X ∪ D and X ∖ D are decidable. To use this, find a decidable D that strips an unknown language X down to a known undecidable one. Syntax is the usual partner. The set of strings that are valid codes of pairs ⟨M,w⟩ is decidable, because a machine can check the format in a bounded number of steps. The second worked problem uses it.

worked_problems.title: Prove that the halting language is undecidable
worked_problems.question: Let HALT_TM = {⟨M,w⟩ : M halts on w}. Assume that A_TM is known to be undecidable. Write a complete proof that HALT_TM is undecidable by building a decider for A_TM from a hypothetical decider H for HALT_TM.
worked_problems.strategy: Put the known-hard language A_TM on the side we want to decide. Use H to remove the looping case, because simulating M is safe only after H has promised that M halts.
steps: Assume H decides HALT_TM. Define S on input ⟨M,w⟩: run H on ⟨M,w⟩.

If H rejects, M loops on w, so M does not accept w, and S rejects. If H accepts, M halts on w, so simulating M on w is sure to finish. S simulates M on w and gives the same answer: accept if M accepts, reject if M rejects.

Correctness: if M accepts w, then H accepts, the simulation accepts, and S accepts. If M rejects w, then H accepts, the simulation rejects, and S rejects. If M loops, then H rejects and S rejects. In every case S accepts exactly when M accepts w.

Termination: H always halts. The simulation starts only after H has said that M halts on w, so it halts too. Hence S halts on every input and decides A_TM, which is impossible. So H does not exist. For example, if M accepts strings with an even number of 1s and w = 1011, then H accepts (M halts after 4 steps), the simulation rejects, and S rejects.
worked_problems.answer: HALT_TM is undecidable. The proof is valid because the only step that might loop, the simulation of M, starts only after H has certified that it halts.
worked_problems.sanity_check: If H were allowed to loop on some inputs, the last step would fail: S might loop too, so S would not be a decider and there would be no contradiction.

worked_problems.title: Use closure to show a padded language is undecidable
worked_problems.question: Let V be the set of strings that are valid codes of the form ⟨M,w⟩. Let X = A_TM ∪ (Σ* ∖ V). So X holds the pairs where M accepts w, together with every string that is not a valid pair code. Prove that X is undecidable, using only that A_TM is undecidable and that V is decidable.
worked_problems.strategy: Assume X is decidable and recover A_TM by intersecting with the decidable set V.
steps: V is decidable: a machine can check the format of a string in a bounded number of steps, then accept or reject. Decidable languages are closed under intersection.
Compute X ∩ V. Every member of A_TM is a valid pair code, so A_TM ∩ V = A_TM. The padding Σ* ∖ V shares nothing with V, so (Σ* ∖ V) ∩ V = ∅. Hence X ∩ V = A_TM.

Suppose X had a decider D_X. Then this machine always halts: on input z, run the format check for V; if z is not valid, reject; otherwise run D_X on z and copy its answer. It decides A_TM. For z = “hello”, the format check fails and the machine rejects, which is right because “hello” is not in A_TM.
That contradicts the undecidability of A_TM, so D_X cannot exist.
worked_problems.answer: X is undecidable. Padding an undecidable language with easy-to-recognize junk does not make it decidable.
worked_problems.sanity_check: The argument needs V to be decidable. If checking the format were itself undecidable, step 1 would fail and the machine in step 3 might not halt.

worked_problems.title: Prove a language unrecognizable with a step-bounded gadget
worked_problems.question: Let ALL_TM = {⟨M⟩ : L(M) = Σ*}. Prove that ALL_TM is not recognizable. You may use that the complement of A_TM is not recognizable.
worked_problems.strategy: Reduce the complement of A_TM to ALL_TM. The gadget must accept every string exactly when M does not accept w, and a step bound makes that possible.
steps: Define f. For a valid pair ⟨M,w⟩, f outputs the code of N, which works as follows on input x: simulate M on w for at most |x| steps; if M has accepted by then, reject; otherwise accept. For a string that is not a valid pair, f outputs the code of a machine that accepts everything. Writing these codes always finishes, so f is computable and defined on every string.
If M does not accept w (it rejects or loops), no simulation ever sees M accept, so N accepts every x and L(N) = Σ*. So f(⟨M,w⟩) is in ALL_TM, and ⟨M,w⟩ is in the complement of A_TM.

If M accepts w after exactly 5 steps, then N rejects every x with |x| ≥ 5 and accepts only the shorter strings, so L(N) ≠ Σ*. So f(⟨M,w⟩) is not in ALL_TM, and ⟨M,w⟩ is not in the complement of A_TM. Invalid strings map into ALL_TM and also lie in the complement. So the two sides always agree.
Suppose Q recognized ALL_TM. Then “compute f, then run Q” would recognize the complement of A_TM, which is impossible. So Q does not exist.
worked_problems.answer: ALL_TM is not recognizable. The step bound is what turns “M accepts w at some time” into “N fails to accept everything.”
worked_problems.sanity_check: If M accepts w after t steps, N rejects exactly the strings of length at least t. For t = 5 that is every string of length 5 or more, so N misses infinitely many strings, as required.

code_examples.title: Build the gadget without running it
code_examples.intro: Emma wants to see the shape of the proof as a program. A toy machine here is a Python generator: every yield is one step, and returning "accept" or "reject" halts it. The function build_Mw is the reduction from the main example. It writes a new machine and runs nothing. A stand-in for the decider R looks for an accepted string within a budget of steps. No real R exists, so the stand-in is only a guess, and the table shows where it goes wrong.
code_examples.code:
# A toy machine is a generator function. Each yield is one step.
# Returning "accept" or "reject" halts it. Never returning means looping.

def run(machine, text, budget):
    """Run for at most `budget` steps. Return the answer, or None if unfinished."""
    steps = machine(text)
    for _ in range(budget):
        try:
            next(steps)
        except StopIteration as done:
            return done.value
    return None


def even_ones(text):                 # accepts when the number of 1s is even
    ones = 0
    for ch in text:
        yield
        ones += ch == "1"
    return "accept" if ones % 2 == 0 else "reject"


def spin(text):                      # loops forever
    while True:
        yield


def slow_accept(text):               # accepts, but only after 5000 steps
    for _ in range(5000):
        yield
    return "accept"


def build_Mw(M, w):
    """The reduction. It writes down a new machine and runs nothing."""
    def Mw(x):
        yield
        if x != w:
            return "reject"
        answer = yield from M(w)     # simulate M on w, one step at a time
        return "accept" if answer == "accept" else "reject"
    return Mw


def stand_in_for_R(machine, probes, budget):
    """A budgeted guess at 'is the language empty?'. A real decider cannot exist."""
    return all(run(machine, p, budget) != "accept" for p in probes)


def S(M, w, budget):
    Mw = build_Mw(M, w)                              # step 1: always finishes
    empty = stand_in_for_R(Mw, [w, "", "0"], budget)  # step 2: ask R
    return not empty                                 # step 3: flip the answer


cases = [("even_ones", even_ones, "1001"), ("even_ones", even_ones, "1011"),
         ("spin", spin, "1001"), ("slow_accept", slow_accept, "1001")]
print("machine      w     M accepts w  R says empty  S accepts  S correct")
for name, M, w in cases:
    truth = run(M, w, 20000) == "accept"
    says = S(M, w, 100)
    print(f"{name:<12} {w}  {str(truth):<11}  {str(not says):<12}  {str(says):<9}  {says == truth}")

print("building M_w for a looping M returns at once:", callable(build_Mw(spin, "1001")))
print("running that M_w on w for 100 steps gives:", run(build_Mw(spin, "1001"), "1001", 100))
code_examples.output:
machine      w     M accepts w  R says empty  S accepts  S correct
even_ones    1001  True         False         True       True
even_ones    1011  False        True          False      True
spin         1001  False        True          False      True
slow_accept  1001  True         True          False      False
building M_w for a looping M returns at once: True
running that M_w on w for 100 steps gives: None
walkthrough: run executes a toy machine for at most budget steps and returns its answer, or None if the machine is still running. A program cannot wait forever, and this models that limit.
even_ones, spin and slow_accept behave differently on every input: one halts with an answer, one loops forever, and one accepts only after 5000 steps.
build_Mw is the reduction. It returns a new machine that rejects every x other than w, and on w it runs M with yield from. Nothing runs when build_Mw is called.
S follows the three steps of the proof: build M_w, ask the stand-in for R whether M_w accepts nothing, and answer the opposite.
The final loop compares S with the truth. The truth column uses a large budget, which works only because we know these toy machines. For real machines it cannot be computed.
code_examples.explanation:
The table shows the logic of S. The stand-in R says “empty” when none of the probe strings is accepted within 100 steps, and S returns the opposite. For the first three rows this matches the truth about M and w. For slow_accept, M does accept w, but only after 5000 steps. Within 100 steps M_w has not accepted yet, the stand-in says “empty”, and S answers wrongly.

Raising the budget fixes this machine and fails on the next, slower one. That is the heart of the theorem in miniature: no fixed amount of waiting can separate a machine that never accepts from a machine that accepts very late. A real decider R would have to be right about every machine, and that is exactly what cannot exist.

The last two lines show why the construction step is safe. Building M_w for a looping machine returns at once, because building only creates a new function. Running that M_w on w never finishes, and the program stops it after 100 steps. The proof never runs M_w. It gives the description to R.

topics.title: Propositional syntax and truth
topics.story:
A laboratory alarm panel combines simple signals: a door is open, a fan is running, and a temperature limit is exceeded. The panel's wiring describes how the signals combine; their current on/off settings determine the resulting alarm value. Logic separates those two layers as syntax and semantics.

Parentheses are like wiring connections: changing them can change what the panel computes. The model assumes each signal has a definite truth value. It does not express measurement uncertainty or causal influence automatically, so a logical implication should not be mistaken for a physical mechanism connecting two sensors.
topics.principle:
Propositional formulas are built from atomic propositions and connectives such as negation, conjunction and disjunction. A truth assignment gives each atom a Boolean value, and the formula's value is computed recursively from its parse tree. Disjunction is inclusive unless exclusive-or is stated. Material implication P→Q is false only when P is true and Q false; when P is false, the implication is true.

A formula is satisfiable if at least one assignment makes it true, valid if every assignment does, and unsatisfiable if none does. With k atoms, a full truth table has 2ᵏ rows. This gives a finite decision procedure, though an exponential number of assignments can be expensive even when evaluating each individual assignment is easy.
topics.formula:
P→Q ≡ ¬P∨Q
Satisfiable F: ∃α, α(F)=1
Valid F: ∀α, α(F)=1
topics.symbols:
P and Q are formulas, F is the formula under examination and α is an assignment of truth values to atoms. α(F) extends that assignment recursively to the whole formula.

The symbols ∃ and ∀ mean “there exists” and “for every.” Here 1 denotes true. The equivalence for implication defines its truth-functional behavior; it does not say that P causes Q or that Q is relevant to P.
topics.example:
Let p mean the sample is refrigerated and q mean its seal is intact. Consider F=p→q. The assignments (p,q)=(false,false), (false,true) and (true,true) satisfy F; only (true,false) falsifies it. Therefore F is satisfiable but not valid. Now add the requirement p, forming p∧(p→q).

The only satisfying assignment has p=true and q=true. If we additionally require ¬q, no assignment remains and the resulting conjunction is unsatisfiable. This stepwise reasoning shows how a set of requirements can rule out configurations without claiming that refrigeration itself physically ensures a seal is intact.
topics.pitfall: Reading “p only if q” as q→p. “Only if” gives a necessary condition, so the correct translation is p→q.

check.question: Is p∨¬p merely satisfiable, or valid?
check.answer: It is valid under classical two-valued semantics: either p is true, or p is false and its negation is true.

glossary.meaning: A choice of true or false for each atomic proposition.
True for at least one assignment.
